subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REVIEW OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT AND THE MERIT PRINCIPLE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43 I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter.
Considering that the Quebec referendum campaign is now under way; considering that federal civil servants, as first-class citizens, will be called upon to participate actively in that campaign; considering that the employment act restricts the political participation of civil servants in the normal election process but gives no indication as to the legality of their active participation in partisan referendum activities; considering that the Progressive Conservative government cannot continue to waffle on this matter and must give clear and specific instructions with regard to this important matter, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Cousineau):

That this House requests the government to amend the Public Service Employment Act and, in doing so, adopt the recommendations of the special committee on the Review of Personnel Management and the Merit Principle so as to allow some public servants to participate freely in political activities during elections and referendum campaigns and, secondly, to allow public servants for whom the duties of their positions vary from the First group, to participate in elections and referendums subject to request by the employee and decisions by the Public Service Commission and, thirdly, to prohibit senior executives and senior management, whose duties can be considered sensitive if they participate in elections or referendum campaigns; the foregoing to allow Canadians working in the public service to participate in good conscience and in defence of their country in the upcoming referendum.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity for which there seems to be support in all parts of the House.
In view of the fact that today the trial of a number of human rights activists begins in Prague, Czechoslovakia, in view of the fact that the activities of these people are apparently the result of a civil rights movement which led to the creation of the movement known under the name of "Charter 77", and in view of the fact that Law No. 120 of the Czechoslovak Collection of Laws of October 13, 1976, includes the text of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, which were signed on behalf of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic in 1968 and confirmed at the 1975 Helsinki Conference, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That this House register with the Parliament of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic, the concern and the hope of the Canadian people that these trials be conducted publicly, be open to observers and that the human and civil rights of those being tried be upheld and respected according to the spirit of the Helsinki Act.

FUTURE PRICE OF OIL-AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In the last two weeks we have attempted, in this House, to get the government to tell the Canadian public what it is entitled to know, that is, the kind of oil price increases with which it is proposing to hit the public. Today we heard stories that an agreement had been reached on the weekend between the minister of energy for Alberta and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The agreement was for a $4 per barrel increase in the price of oil, which would mean that the average Canadian consumer will be taxed an additional $180 for gas and home heating oil next year.
My question is as follows: Can the minister tell the House whether an agreement or understanding, formal or informal, has been reached with the government of Alberta? Is the agreement for an unbelievable $4 a barrel more next year and, if that is not so, what were the exact Figures arrived at between the two ministers on the weekend?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. companies with regard to the price increases he is about to announce, and have they given him assurance that the additional revenues which will accrue to them will be used in Canada for exploration and development in the energy field?

Mr. Speaker, the fact is that there has been broadly-based consultation with all segments of the industry, including representatives from CPA and 1PAC. We have had consultation at the official level. I have met with them myself and discussed energy policy and the implications of that energy policy and energy self-sufficiency.
We will require the co-operation of Canadian and foreign corporations in this country in order to achieve our goal of energy self-sufficiency. In fact, a monitoring process has been taking place in respect of the profits of the oil companies, and this indicates that something in the vicinity of 95 per cent of the profits of the oil companies has been reinvested in Canada.
Our intention is to encourage that kind of investment, and we will try as much as possible to bring all elements, both in respect of private industry and government involvement in that direction as well, to assure and reassure that all the resources we have in Canada are pointed toward the achievement of energy self-sufficiency in Canada, so we will not be subject to the very questionable offshore import requirements that we would face down the road if we carried out the policy enunciated by the hon. member's colleague, the critic for energy of the Liberal party.

Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the right hon. Prime Minister and member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) is out of order, and I remind hon. members of the terms of that motion:
That a committee be appointed to prepare and report, in accordance with Standing Order 65, lists of members to compose the standing and standing joint committees of this House; and that the committee be composed of Messrs. Baker (Nepean-Carleton), Kempling, Friesen, MacEachen, Lefebvre and Knowles, and that the provisions of Standing Order 65(1) be suspended in relation to the number of members on the said committee.
That is where, Mr. Speaker, 1 say this motion is not receivable, as the motion itself talks about suspending a provision of the Standing Orders. Indeed, the authors are unanimous, Mr. Speaker: suspending a provision of the Standing Orders requires unanimity or a notice on the order paper and, as you know, a notice of this kind cannot be put on the order paper the first day of the opening of the session since under parliamentary law that day is not considered as a regular day of sitting. That is why that very motion to suspend a rule of the House could not be put on the first day of the session. I quote an authority on parliamentary law, A. Beauchesne, citation 13, at page 7, on unanimous consent:
Point of Order-Mr. F. Roy
13. 1) Within the ambit of its own rules, the House itself may proceed as it chooses; it is a common practice for the House to ignore its own rules by unanimous consent. Thus, bills may be passed through all their stages in one day, or the House may decide to alter its normal order of business or its adjournment hour as it sees fit.
2) The House is perfectly able to give consent to set aside its Standing Orders and to give its unanimous consent-
You will have noticed, Mr. Speaker, "and to give its unanimous consent"-
-to waive procedural requirements and precedents concerning notice and things of that sort.
Mr. Speaker, I would like now to quote from Bourinot, on page 214:
Each House is bound by every consideration of self-interest and justice to observe strictly its rules and Standing Orders, and to rebuke-
I repeat "to rebuke-"
-every attempt to evade or infringe them.
Consequently, the Senate and the House of Commons never permit-
Mr. Speaker, it is well defined in Bourinottheir rules and Standing Orders to be suspended, unless by unanimous consent.
Mr. Speaker, I can never overemphasize the necessity to comply with the rules. All authorities are explicit on that point, and allow me to quote again from Erskine May.
Here is what we find in the chapter
Breaches of Privilege and Contempts-
-under the heading
Disobedience to Rules or Orders of either House
Disobedience to the orders of either House, whether such orders are of general application or require a particular individual to do or abstain from doing a particular act, or contravention of any rules of either House is a contempt of that House.
Those are not the words of the hon. member for Beauce. I am simply quoting from the experts in parliamentary procedure.
The rules of this House are in contempt of Parliament, especially when one considers the origins of the Standing Orders. I should like to quote once more from Bourinot in his chapter on the rules and regulations, in the section on the origin of the rules, where we find the following:
To protect the minority and restrain the improvidence and tyranny of the majority-
-even though there is not absolute majority in the House-
-to secure the transaction of public business in a decent and orderly manner.
Mr. Speaker, this is what we find when we refer to the various experts.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not criticizing anything that you have
said or done. Indeed, from the very beginning of the discussion

on the motion in question, you said "pursuant to the provisions of the Standing Orders", and you then asked for the vote.
However, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my motion was actually to try to obtain the unanimous consent of the House in order to straighten out the matter.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, you could not foresee the result of the vote. Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer you to the term of Standing Order 51, and I quote:
Whenever Mr. Speaker is of the opinion that a motion offered to the House is contrary to the rules and privileges of Parliament...
-and I am doing just this-
-he shall apprise the House thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon-
... if a vote is in fact required, before putting the question thereon . . .
... and quote the Standing Order or authority applicable to the case.
Mr. Speaker, it is therefore your duty to inform the House that an order has been taken contrary to our rules.
Mr. Speaker, what are the possible avenues? Since that famous April 2, 1604, even if they have the power, members have always been reluctant to rescind theirs orders. This stands from the judicial nature of the British-type parliament.
We therefore recommend that an order do issue declaring the proceedings null and void. We find in May the following quote:
That an order do issue declaring procedures to be null and void where procedures have been violated, even inadvertently.
-and I quote specifically Mr. Erskine May:
An order declaring proceedings to be null and void is employed where there has been an inadvertence or some form of irregularity in procedure (u). The reason for resorting to it is either (i) that there is no resolution which can be rescinded or order which can be discharged
And Mr. Erskine May goes on to say:
The proceedings are declared null and void.
Since the British House of Commons in similar circumstances does this, and I am referring to the three dates I have given earlier in my remarks, when emphasizing that this is how they had proceeded on February 23, 1939 by declaring the carried motions null and void, they did the same on May 21, 1957 and again on April 25, 1963.
As in the case of all the other rulings, this last case is interesting because all proceedings following an irregularity were declared null and void.

[Mr. Roy (Beauce).1

speakeroldname: Hon. John A. Fraser (Postmaster General and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last week a scientific report was released, and as a consequence some members of the House asked that a statement respecting the present government position on acid rain be made in the House. I agreed to make that statement, and as a consequence I am here today.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. May I ask whether copies of this statement have been given in advance to the spokesmen on this issue for the other parties?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that in both cases statements were given in advance. I am surprised that the hon. member who raised the issue in the House of Commons is not here this afternoon, and I have no explanation for that.
The gradual increase in acidity of precipitation in eastern North America and in Europe has been of concern to the scientific community for some time. It was not, however, until the findings of an OECD study were released in 1976 that the potential magnitude and seriousness of the problem in western Europe were first grasped by a wider public. The concern was carried to all of Europe through the implementation of a scientific study under the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe. Indeed, next month numerous European countries, as well as Canada and the United States, are expected to sign a convention on long-range transboundary air pollution which was developed last year under the ECE. This convention represents the first step being taken to address the problem of acid rain in Europe and is indicative of the concern for the problem. While the Government of Canada actively participated in the development of the convention, the convention is very general in nature and is insufficient to deal with the situation in eastern North America.
Early awareness of a potential acid rain problem in eastern North America was heightened by the OECD report. Recognizing that convincing presumptive evidence indicated that the long-range transport of a variety of polluting substances, particularly acid pollutants, was undoubtedly occurring within and into Canada, Environment Canada embarked on a comprehensive scientific program to develop a clearer understanding of all aspects of the complex problem.
Members of the House will recall that in June 1977 the then minister of fisheries and environment gave a strongly worded speech to the Air Pollution Control Association meeting in Toronto in which he referred to the problem of acid rain as an "environmental time bomb". The speech was aimed at focusing the attention of the federal and provincial governments on the problem and indicating Canadian concern for the first time to the United States. With the increased knowledge which we have acquired in the past two years, it is now evident that the time bomb is much bigger than anything envisaged in 1977.
Recognizing the international dimensions of the problem and the need for international co-operation in the development of a mutually agreed scientific data base from which to

October 22, 1979
Acid Rain
develop solutions, the Government of Canada and the United States in 1978 established the Canada-United States bilateral research consultation group. The initial results from Environment Canada's scientific program, together with results from provincial and United States scientific investigations, were described in the first report of this group which was released on Monday. The report indicates that large areas of North America are sensitive to damage from acidic precipitation.
Decreased productivity and diversity of fish species have been observed in lakes and rivers in Ontario and in the Atlantic provinces. While we do not have as detailed data for Quebec, there is every reason to believe that the situation is similar in that province. Spawning failure of Atlantic salmon in streams in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces has been linked to acid precipitation. The precise extent of the damage being done is difficult to determine but the continually emerging evidence indicates ever more serious concerns, as well as increasing geographical extent. For example, various pieces of evidence suggest agricultural and forest productivity are at risk. While some of the potential damage cannot be irrefutably proven at present, by the time it has manifested itself the damage could be irreversible.
Continued pollutant loading of sensitive areas of eastern Canada at present levels will result in continued degradation with extensive irreversible acidification occurring during the next decade or so, particularly in aquatic ecosystems. Increased loading will accelerate the rate of deterioration. The report also notes extensive damage in the northeastern part of the United States where there is strong concern about the problem.
In anticipation of the contents of the research consultation group report and aware that the situation was serious, the Government of Canada and the United States issued a joint statement and communique on transboundary air pollution on July 26, 1979. In these documents the two governments outlined the basis of existing co-operation and indicated their intention to develop a co-operative agreement on transboundary air quality. The release of the joint statement and communique followed meetings of officials from both countries on December 15, 1978, and June 20, 1979.
While I welcomed the work which had been done in this regard by officials of my department and the Department of External Affairs, I recognized that a commitment at the highest level was needed to set in motion the reduction in emissions necessary to ameliorate the problem. On August 8, 1979 I went to Washington and met with the hon. Cecil Andrus, Secretary of the Interior, the hon. Douglas Costle, Administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and the hon. Gus Speth, Chairman of the President's Council on Environmental Quality. I made it clear to my U.S. colleagues that the Government of Canada attaches a very high priority to the rapid reduction of acid-causing pollutants. I emphasized the fact that both countries were polluting each other and that effective control could best be undertaken on a co-operative basis.

I found complete acceptance of this view and a willingness to examine specific strategies designed to put in place the needed controls. I undertook to accelerate the process of developing with the provinces concerned appropriate Canadian control strategies and I was assured that a similar effort will be made in the United States. The next Canada-U.S. meeting on acid rain, this time involving both federal and provincial officials, takes place October 24 in Washington. Needless to say, this important matter also will be discussed during President Carter's visit to Ottawa November 9 and 10.
Immediately following my return from the United States I met with Dr. Parrott, the Ontario minister of the environment. 1 was much heartened by this meeting. We have a mutual understanding of the importance of the problem and a desire to address the necessary solutions. Dr. Parrott made it clear that Ontario will apply diligently any requirements agreed by the Canadian and U.S. governments in a future agreement. I will be meeting with Mr. Leger soon and I hope to achieve a similar understanding with him on the need for action. I have spoken to Mr. Bacon of Nova Scotia who is also the current chairman of the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers. I recognize the importance of discussing this matter with other provincial colleagues as well.
A federal-provincial committee on control strategies for long-range transport of air pollutants has been set up to focus on solutions to the acid rain problem. This committee originally contained provincial representatives from Ontario and Quebec only. Its formation was strongly endorsed at the June 1979 meeting of the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, and Nova Scotia, as current CCREM chairman, was added to represent the other provinces. The CCREM recognized the seriousness of the problem, endorsed federal leadership in seeking solutions and gave strong support to the federal government in undertaking negotiations with the United States.
The focal point of the committee's first meeting on September 25 was a conceptual work plan of the tasks necessary to identify, develop and evaluate alternative abatement strategies. The plan is designed to provide recommendations to governments of the cost effectiveness of various control options. I am pleased to report that there was agreement on the general thrust of the plan by all in attendance. Despite the complicated nature of the problem, and competing environmental, economic and social factors, the initial output of this activity should be available by spring.
This initial output, which would assess the application of specific abatement technologies with preliminary cost estimates, would not however tell us much about specific environmental benefits that might result from a particular level of reduction. It would take much longer to produce precise data for this purpose although clearer understandings of effects are continually emerging. The extent to which we need precise data on expected environmental benefits would depend in part on how costly the controls might be. Similarly, should the direct control costs appear very high, extensive additional economic analysis designed to help us understand the broader
October 22, 1979

effects of these costs on society would be needed to guide us in selecting the optimum means of control. For these reasons it is not yet possible to estimate with certainty the time needed before firm recommendations for ultimate control strategies will be forthcoming.
Let me illustrate further. Members will be aware of some early general estimates made by my officials suggesting that a 50 per cent reduction of emissions of sulphur dioxide in eastern Canada would result in direct costs to polluters of $350 million to $500 million annually over the remainder of the century.
The figures which have yet to undergo detailed analysis do not, for example, take account of possible offsets arising from the effective marketing of by-product sulphuric acid in Canada or for export, nor do they reflect impacts on other sectors of society ranging from electricity bills to balance of payments. Obviously informed judgments will have to be made about these matters before committing ourselves to a particular course of action. Elowever, lest I be misunderstood, let me make it perfectly clear that there will have to be major reductions in the release of acid causing pollutants in North America, and this government is determined to ensure that Canada meets this challenge.
As I have indicated in several statements on this subject, it is our present intention to rely on the provinces to put in place the needed control requirements. I am counting on my provincial colleagues and I am confident that they will do what must be done. However, members of the House have asked what will the federal government do should the provinces fail to act. The federal government has the constitutional authority to act for the good of the country in respect of controlling the interprovincial and international flow of pollutants. We would not shrink from this responsibility. Indeed, it is very much my view that the federal government ought to have at least residual authority set out in legislation to deal, as needed, with interprovincial and international pollution problems, which is something we currently do not have, in both the air and water fields. I have instructed my officials to examine this matter in the context of our current review of the federal government's role in environmental protection.
Given the time sensitivity of the issue, it is obviously important to look at interim measures to retard the problem. While it is not clear at this time what these might be, I have instructed my officials to investigate all possibilities. As an absolute minimum 1 believe it would only be wise to ensure that there be no further increase in emissions of sulphur dioxide in central and eastern Canada. 1 will be discussing this with my provincial colleagues. In addition, I plan to hold discussions with the chief executive officers of the corporations in Canada principally responsible for the problem.
Members of the House are fully aware that, however rigorous our domestic control strategy may be, it cannot alone overcome all the effects of acid rain. May I therefore conclude by stating that I have instructed my officials to ensure that, in co-operation with the provinces, all of the necessary preparato-
Acid Rain
ry work is completed in time to allow signature of an effective Canada-U.S. abatement agreement as soon as possible after the U.S. election next year.
Throughout this century Canada and the United States have led the world in effectively dealing with transboundary pollution, whether in water or air. In this the provinces have consistently been our partners. 1 am confident that this longstanding partnership, both domestic and international, will continue.

Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House we thank the minister for his thoughtfulness in providing us with a copy of his statement this morning, and we also wish to congratulate him on his decision to make a statement on acid rain in this House and to hear the comments and questions of interested parliamentarians.
We agree with the minister that the situation is very serious and that we are dealing here with what has been described as an "environmental time bomb". Here ends the positive part of our message on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, and I will explain briefly why.
If, as in the words of the minister, "the damage could be irreversible", and there are indications in the environment that this could be the case, then several questions come to mind as to why this government is tackling the matter of acid rain so slowly. For instance, why did six weeks go by from the date when the minister came back from Washington before the first meeting was held by the federal-provincial committee on control strategies for long-range transport of air pollutants? Why is it that the initial output of the work of this committee can only be available next spring? Why, two and a half months after the minister's visit to Washington, is there no indication in his statement today of the specifics of the Canadian control strategies, on the eve of the next Canada-U.S. meeting on acid rain scheduled to take place this coming Wednesday? Why has a meeting not yet taken place between the minister and his counterpart in the province of Quebec?
Why, considering the gravity of the situation described by the minister himself, is there hesitancy, to say the least, in making the polluters pay by charging them the estimated cost of $350 million to $500 million annually, or any sum for that matter?
Why does the committee on control strategies for long-range transport of air pollutants, which supposedly reports to the minister-and we hope the deliberations of this committee will not be as long as its name-have to be concerned with "the cost effectiveness of various control options", when life around us-the ponds, brooks, rivers, lakes and perhaps even our fields and forests-is being poisoned to the point where human health might be affected too, in the long run?
Really, what is $350 million annually if we are to deal with this "time bomb" described by the minister? What is $350 million today if, by all estimates, costs can only increase if action is delayed?
Why is it that if, as he says today, the minister thinks he can
prevent present levels of pollutants causing acid rain from

October 22, 1979
Acid Rain
increasing, the technology needed to do this cannot be used to decrease levels of emission? Why cannot his so-called "interim measures" be used to decrease levels of emission if they can be used to prevent increases?
Why is it that the minister informs us again today that the signing of the agreement has to wait for a new president to be installed, 16 months from now, when by all accounts President Carter is a well-known politician for his commitment to the cause of a clean environment?
What is at stake here, Mr. Speaker, and not in respect of acid rain alone, is the credibility of the political system at the international, national and provincial levels, namely, whether or not in the eyes of the public we, the elected representatives, are capable of delivering in response to the gravity of a situation threatening the survival of the ecology of our planet.
We on this side of the House cannot believe or accept that the concern of U.S. citizens vis-a-vis acid rain is any less than that of Canadians. We on this side of the House cannot believe or accept that the concern of residents of Ontario is any less than that of residents of Quebec or of the Atlantic provinces.
If elected representatives in provincial legislatures and their governments engage in jurisdictional games instead of offering their fullest co-operation, they do so at their own political peril and will have to be judged by their own constituents accordingly. While acid rain continues to do its insidious damage, we cannot wait for jurisdictional duels to take place at the peril of our environment. The solution to a serious threat to our environment, which as we all know unfortunately knows no boundaries, cannot be allowed to become the victim of ineptly handled federal-provincial relations.
On the other hand, there is ample evidence, at least in this House today, that the minister and members of all parties are very worried about this invisible death creeping around us. What we cannot understand then, given these elements of urgency and the desire to co-operate, is why the responsible officials, be they provincial or be they federal on both sides of the border, cannot be locked up in a conference room and given, say, 60 days to come up with standards required and with the text of an agreement for the signature of the U.S. president and our Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). Representatives from industry and from labour could be added so as to facilitate and expedite the work of these officials.
The minister's statement today reminds us of someone who, at the site of a burning building, cried "Fire!" but tells the occupants they have to wait a year and a half for the fire trucks to come to their rescue.
Canadians, as we all know, are in the forefront of all nations as being known for their sensitivity to the quality of their environment. They cannot be reassured by the government's actions so far and by today's statement, because the minister has not been able to explain why we have to wait so long for the United States and, in an equally serious matter, why we have to wait so long for the provinces to move and to take vigorous action, particularly-and on this I will conclude-in the light of this passage contained in the long-range transport

of air pollutants report, which is at the base of today's statement and which states on page 25 that "the greater portion of total sulphur deposition in each country is probably the result of domestic emissions".

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to thank the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Fraser) for getting his statement to my office well in advance of question period today. Also, I would like to thank him for the detail of the statement which runs approximately ten pages in length.
A lot has been said and written about acid rain in recent weeks and months. I will be brief in my response and concentrate on asking the minister if he would do everything in his power to get some action from this moment on, instead of speeches, words and statements to the press. In saying that, I am not levelling my criticism directly at the new minister responsible for the environment, as was alleged or stated a few moments ago by the member from one of the Toronto ridings. After all, the previous administration was well aware of the implications and the most serious fears with respect to acid rain fall-out for approximately a year, the last year that they were in office.
I would like to state at this point that I believe it is grossly unfair for a Liberal member of this House to condemn outright, or to a considerable degree, the present administration when in fact his own party had plenty of time to investigate and bring in some remedies.
Hear, hear!

Having said that, I would like to reiterate once again what has been said in this House with respect to the seriousness of acid rain itself. As the minister knows, it is the most serious environmental threat that we have today in Canada and in North America. Indeed, it is very common in central and western Europe and in Scandinavia. Acid rain is a very insidious thing in that one cannot see it, taste it, touch it or smell it. It is not like the Don River in Toronto oozing its sludge into Lake Ontario; you can see and smell it and say, "Yes, that is pollution."
None of these elements are available to the human senses. Therefore, it is difficult to marshal public opinion as well as corporate action with respect to acid rain because, as I have discovered in the last few weeks, most people are not even aware that it exists, and therefore are not aware of the horrendous potential damage that it may have for all of us.
In the province of Ontario alone we have lost approximately 140 lakes as far as aquatic life is concerned. They are what we call dead lakes, yet they still look very attractive. The water looks very clear and one can go boating and sailing, but the sport fishing industry is finished in those lakes. When one looks at the statistics with respect to sport fishing and angling in Ontario, one discovers that of a $600 million a year tourist industry approximately half of the income relates directly to sport fishing. The other half, of course, is divided up among winter sports, such as hunting, skiing and such.
October 22, 1979

If this acid rain situation continues, we will lose virtually all our lakes in Ontario and most of the lakes in Quebec. Time is running out. However, it may not be until the most serious consequences of acid rain are known that the public will really become angry if the government does not act and act very quickly. I am referring to the report that was released, I believe, just last week, the joint report of Canadian-United States scientists in which they are now discovering that acid rain is definitely having irreversible effects, limited as they may be, at the present, on crops through the soil. The effects on the soil will lead to crop reduction.
At this point I would like to put a question to the minister which he perhaps will answer in a few moments after he has had a few moments to think about it, if he has not already. It has come to my attention informally that the Athabasca tar sands are posing a very serious sulphuric threat to the Canadian breadbasket, the prairies, in so far as grain production is concerned. The threat is not in the immediate sense, but unless something is done about the Athabasca tar sands emission of sulphuric acid into the atmosphere- because as the minister knows, it does not have to rain down; it can simply fall down out of the atmosphere on to the Canadian prairies-it could become a serious threat.
Think of the magnitude and the consequences if we were to allow the Canadian prairies, and no doubt the American plain states, to become wastelands while we dither, talk and argue as to whether or not it is a provincial responsibility or a Canadian federal initiative and whether or not President Carter is running or not running for re-election. The whole thing becomes not only serious, but could foster cynicism because of the political implications of the whole problem.
The minister has outlined a rough time frame. He has not been specific. No doubt he cannot be specific in terms of actual dates, days or weeks or months, but I implore the minister, as he states in his statement, to use the powers that the federal government presently has. 1 implore the minister not to wait for Dr. Parrott and to stop listening to Inco executives telling him, "Us poor folks up here in Sudbury just can't afford emission control standards or else we will have to lay off two or three thousand Inco workers", all of which is balderdash and Dr. Parrott should know that. 1 am rather disgusted at Dr. Parrott's statements as quoted in the press last week.
The minister's statement at page 8 reads:
The federal government has the constitutional authority to act for the good of the country with respect to controlling the interprovincial and international flow of pollutants.
The minister admits in this statement that he can take the initiative. We on this side of the House and, indeed, the whole country is waiting for the minister to take that initiative. What I would like to suggest is that he begin here in our own backyard in Ontario by calling in the chief executive officer of Inco and saying, "Look, give me your timeframe for cleaning up the emissions".
The Ontario Conservative government has allowed these emissions to continue at the rate of 3,600 metric tons a day
Acid Rain
coming out of the Inco smelters, when it should be down to 750 metric tons a day, which is still disastrous. Yet Dr. Parrott at Queen's Park says, "Well, we can't force them because we don't want to do anything to upset Ottawa-Washington negotiations on this matter, so we will just sit back and go easy with Inco or any other polluter in the province of Ontario until my federal counterpart has done all the work with his counterpart in Washington". In other words, Parrott, I think, is being a Pontius Pilate and simply washing his hands of the whole thing, at least for the time being.
I repeat, time is of the essence in respect to acid rain. No doubt there will be questions asked by other members. In closing, I implore the minister to call in the chief executive officer of Inco and ask him for a timeframe for clean-up. If it is not satisfactory to the minister responsible for the environment, then let the minister bring into the House the necessary legislation. I can assure him that it will be given very fast passage as far as members on this side are concerned.

Acid Rain

Mr. Speaker, I must say the statement by the minister concerning acid rain and the impact it is having on our country is a very sobering one. speechtext:
that Bill C-6, to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure indeed that I rise on second reading of this bill in the House. The amendments to the Old Age Security Act contained in this bill fulfil a clear commitment made by the members on this side during the last election.
There are two parts to the bill. Both deal with the removal of certain provisions contained in the Old Age Security Act which were the source of financial hardship and despair to people affected by it.
The first and broadest amendment deals with the spouse's allowance program. This bill will remove the provision whereby the allowance is cut off six months after the pensioner spouse dies. Up to now the spouse's allowance program has led financially dependent persons into a false sense of security on the basis of income received under the program. Then, at a time when their personal bereavement is still fresh, and their financial prospects have, if anything, dimmed, the financial rug was pulled out from under them.
I am proud to say that this government will no longer tolerate this situation. Within this bill is contained an amendment which will ensure that a person receiving the spouse's allowance will never again have to worry about losing it simply because the older pensioner spouse has passed away. As long as he or she continues to be in need, the continued protection of the spouse's allowance program will be assured.
There is another part to this bill. It is not nearly so significant as the spouse's allowance amendment in terms of the number of persons involved, but in its own way it is also very important. I am referring, of course, to the removal of the provision whereby old age security benefits are suspended if the recipient is sentenced to prison for a term of over 90 days.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that it was announced in the Speech from the Throne that the government will be inviting a parliamentary committee to review the retirement income needs of Canadians in the 1980s. This announcement reflects the fact that this government regards the pensions as a priority area.

October 22, 1979

I want at this time to review in brief some of the issues which have led us to look at pensions in this light. First of all, 1 want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, this House and all Canadians that this government, while it will be seeking efficiency and economy in government, will nevertheless have a strong interest in the social policy sector. In particular, we want to alleviate the situation of low-income Canadians, and our senior citizens certainly have more than their share of persons in the lower income levels. Broadly speaking, we are after a pension system that provides adequate income protection and fair treatment to all.
More specifically, the issues include the difficult situation faced by many old age pensioners; second, the level of protection provided to women by the pension system; third, the performance of the private sector in the pension system; fourth, the introduction of greater flexibility in the age of retirement; fifth, the position of the disabled and the handicapped in the pension system; finally, the protection offered the families of deceased persons, and, for all of these, the maintenance of the purchasing power of benefits paid out.
In reviewing these issues, we will not be starting without some background. We will be drawing upon the numerous pension studies and reports conducted at all levels of society in the last several years. We will be consolidating this information and adding to it from extensive consultation with people in general, with the pension industry, with provincial governments and with special interest groups.
We are all well aware of the review that has been going on for the past three years. That was an interdepartmental study carried out largely by officials under the last government. We in this new government recognize the value of that study as a major background piece of work that has been done, and we will take whatever advantage there is in it although we will not be bound by it.
There are other groups in the pension field to whose work we will be referring, such as the "COFIRENTES" report from the province of Quebec, the Ontario royal commission, the Economic Council of Canada and the Senate committee on retirement age. The federal and provincial ministers of finance have also been sponsoring a study by their governments during the past few years of the funding of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. "Canada at the Pension Crossroads" by the Research Foundation of Financial Executives Institute and "Pensions and Survival" by Geoffrey Calvert are just two of the studies conducted in the private sector.
I want to stress in discussing the process which I am describing that this government will be looking at the pension sector with a fresh perspective. If this review should reveal that a major overhaul of the pension system is necessary to create an effective, fair and efficient structure, then we will be free to develop and carry out such an overhaul.
Nor is this process going to be strictly related to the bureaucracy or even the government alone. In keeping with the open government policies of this side of the House, we want to involve Parliament in the process through the participation of a parliamentary committee. The members of this committee
Old Age Security
will be able to reach out to Canadians on particular issues in the pension field and obtain and evaluate views from every part of the land and from very broad terms of reference.
Great emphasis will be placed upon consultation and cooperation with the provinces and the private sector. By this means we will be able to seek joint solutions which we can all accept as being the best avenues for meeting the future pension needs of Canadians.
In this context, let me refer again to the specific provisions before us. While this bill may represent a small step, it is an important one for those who will benefit from it, and it is important also to demonstrate this government's concerns for the pension sector in general, and for the problems faced by Canadian women in particular. I look upon this bill as an expression of good faith by this government that what can be done quickly will be done.
When I speak of continued spouse's allowance protection, I do not just mean the continuation of the same amount of benefit payable before. It is significant that over 85 per cent of our spouse's allowance recipients receive less than maximum benefits because they or their spouse have some income aside from old age security benefits. For most of these couples the income received is money coming to the older pensioner spouse, money which will drop dramatically or cease altogether if the older spouse dies. Clearly, it is unrealistic and unjust to continue to pay the same amount of allowance after the spouse's death when we know the allowance recipient's other income has considerably dropped.
For this reason, the spouse's allowance for widowed recipients will not only be extended but will also be recalculated on the basis of the personal income of the surviving spouse-the actual income which he or she has available to meet daily living expenses. The extended allowance will continue to be paid until the beneficiary reaches age 65-when the regular old age security pension is available-or until he or she remarries or dies.
I expect that some 2,200 allowance recipients will receive extended benefits in 1980-81 as a result of these provisions. The cost will be about $4.3 million in that fiscal year or some 2.7 per cent of the total cost of the spouses' allowance program.
This provision will go far in ensuring some financial security for a very vulnerable segment of our society, the newly bereaved, near aged widow. The vast majority of our spouse's allowance recipients are women, many of whom have been out of the paid labour force for years, and others who never sought paid employment. At the age of 60-plus it is clearly unreasonable to assume that they would be able to go out and fully sustain themselves on the labour market.
If I may refer now to the provision which will end the suspension of the OAS benefits for prisoners, this is also an improvement of some significance. 1 might point out that when an OAS pensioner has the pension suspended, any allowance paid to that pensioner's spouse must also be suspended.

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
This is a problem which has been raised by many in this House but in particular I would like to thank the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) for her strong stand on the matter during the last session.
This provision has, over the course of years, proven both difficult and unfair. When OAS pensioners are imprisoned and their benefits are subject to suspension, any delay in effecting the suspension can result in overpayments which must be collected when the pension is released. Even if there is no overpayment, the lack of benefits during imprisonment can mean that these people are released with little money at an advanced age and few prospects for making a living.
There are fewer than 100 persons affected by this provision in any given year. The cost of maintaining payment of their OAS benefits is a small fraction of a per cent of program costs. However, if even one prisoner is able to find a better life as a result of this change, and one prisoner's spouse is not deprived of her allowance, it will be well worth the effort.
In conclusion, I look upon this bill as a first step which this government intends to take, while considering other possibilities for achieving an improved pension system in this country. I invite the support of all members of this House for this particular step, to improve the humanity of a program now in place, and for the broader examination which we hope to carry out, in co-operation with provincial governments and the private sector, to ensure that we have the best possible pension system that we can afford to provide retirement protection for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by congratulating the new minister on the presentation of his first legislation in this House. I express the hope that this will be the first of many. Meanwhile, I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) will clarify the minister's mandate. We on this side keep hearing about ministers responsible for the social policy envelope. There is now to be a super minister of social development. We hope very much that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie), who is responsible for a very major slice of the budget voted by this Parliament, will occupy a very senior position and be heard by his colleagues.

I may say that if the new minister has a slight nervousness, this is shared by his critic. The other day the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) commented on the fact I had moved into a new field. I must confess that the more I read about this field, the more I think it would have been wiser to stay with fisheries and oceans for a while yet. Be that as it may, I am gratified that I have the support and share the co-chairmanship with my colleague, the former minister of national health and welfare, the hon. member for Saint-Leon-ard-Anjou (Miss Begin). She brought, as did her predecessor, the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde), a level of awareness and discussion on social policy matters which I hope to rival.
I might also say that physically located in the House on my left is the formidable veteran for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), an expert to whom we will listen very carefully.

Mr. Speaker, first I must say that we have very few reservations concerning Bill C-6, which will help an important group of our population. At the committee stage, we will put some questions of detail and make some suggestions and I am sure that a number of my colleagues in the House will want to voice their opinion. The fact is that this bill, as the minister admitted himself, is only a first step. It is a modest effort to better the situation of some 2,400 Canadians, according to the figures I saw. However, there is no doubt that this bill will leave many Canadians between 60 and 65 years of age with the impression that they are not treated fairly.

When this legislation was introduced by this party while in office, it was made clear that this spouse's allowance bill was to be seen in the context of a guaranteed annual income program. This in fact was a first step toward this goal. When he was minister of national health and welfare in 1975, the hon. member for Outremont undertook a massive series of consultations with the provinces to achieve this end. Two provinces, Ontario and Alberta, both with Tory provincial governments, prevented the establishment of the basic guaranteed income plan.
It is not without interest that I found in the clippings a quote in the Calgary Herald of December 22, 1977 by the then leader of the opposition, now Prime Minister. The last sentence reads:
So our present plan is certainly not to proceed with a guaranteed annual income program or even to propose one.
There is no doubt that the unfair features of this program would have been and could still be corrected by an enlightened approach in the area of guaranteed income. It is still the basic position of this party that a guaranteed income plan or a plan using the approach of negative income tax is highly desirable. As was the case in medicare, slow progress should not mean that we abandoned the goal we want to reach.
The first group in this country which has a form of guaranteed income are senior citizens over 65 years who are eligible for the guaranteed income supplement. The next obvious
October 22, 1979

group are those between 60 and 65, especially women, whose earnings power and training and educational opportunities are often limited. This is the group with which we should now be concerned.
It is important to remember that the citizens who are now in their early sixties were the teenagers of the depression, a time when educational opportunities outside the cities were meager, if existent at all, when training for women was extremely limited and often those young people who did not serve in the forces, which was the majority, went into jobs which became obsolete and where opportunities for advancement, for such things as private pensions, and so on, were almost unheard of.
These workers were the sons of the marginal farmers in depressed fishing villages, the sons of unskilled workers in our cities. At present they number approximately one million and, according to the statistics 1 have seen, almost 50 per cent of them would require some assistance under an income tested benefit plan.
The government today introduced a bill which would distribute some $4 million to approximately 2,400 Canadians. It is a small step and we hope the minister will come forward with more measures. We hope he will have access to more funds. In fact, he has contributed to his own argument in an article of July 14, 1979 in the Ottawa Journal when he said:
I'm opposed to any plot to dimish the amount spent on the social well-being of citizens.
Spending on health and welfare is not swollen beyond its rightful place.
To which we say, "hear, hear" to the minister. We hope he will pass that clipping around to some of his colleagues. Not only will we support the minister when he brings forward new plans, but we will support him when some of the social programs will be under attack, as they have already been, by some who would sacrifice them on the altar of Tory dogma. In fact, it may be that the minister will want to look to this side for support, and he will have that support when the time comes to arrest the efforts at mutilating some of the social programs, in particular medicare, child credit, family allowances and old age pensions.
After years of effort by successive governments-and Liberal ones have been in office during the passage of most of these major pieces of legislation-there are still, in spite of all these efforts, thousands of people in Canada who live under the poverty line, whatever definition or yardstick is used.
If the Minister of National Health and Welfare brings forth legislation such as Bill C-6, we will support him, even if we do not feel that it goes far enough. As I said earlier, some of my colleagues will suggest some improvement, some changes, that the minister might want to consider.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude this brief statement, my first as critic of social affairs, with a quotation from the great writer and philosopher Georges Bernanos who wrote admirably on world poverty, at a time when it was even worse

than it is now. When somebody came to him with the following objection: "But you forget, sir, that the poor will always be with us", he answered simply: "Yes, alas, they will always be. But the question is to know who will choose them".

Mr. Speaker, may I begin my remarks today by extending my congratulations to the minister not only on introducing this, his first piece of legislation, but on his being invited by the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) to take charge of one of the most important departments in the federal government, the Department of National Health and Welfare. At this point I want also to welcome my friend, the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. LeBlanc), to this very important field. I look forward to his assistance on social matters along the lines he has already indicated in his remarks today.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare described this bill very well when he said it was a small step. Sir, we shall support Bill C-6 although we shall try to have it amended in committee in one or two respects. However, even if we do not get those amendments, we shall support the bill as it is a step in the right direction, as has been said. It does something for about 180 persons a month, and anything that does something for six persons a day is worth taking the time of Parliament to pass.
However, even with all the good will 1 feel toward the minister because he is in this important department and is trying hard, I simply cannot let him get away with the notion that he is doing something wonderful in the bill he has brought forward today. It is so small a step that he must really have been embarrassed in putting it forward.
In a moment I shall explain why I am critical of the government's going only this far, but before I do so I want to say that 1 welcomed the minister's use of a certain phrase when he was talking about improvements in our pensions and social legislation. 1 think his words were: "We want to keep alive the humanity of a program already in place." That is true. In spite of all the faults and shortcomings there might be in the Old Age Security Act, in the Canada Pension Plan, the family allowance program, the unemployment insurance program, and all the rest, we have, in the course of 40 years or 50 years, built a certain amount of humanity into our social programs; and what is most important is that we have made them programs which are such that people do not feel a stigma when they receive the benefits.
I know that, perhaps more often than is comfortable, I have spoken about the days which I remember when a person who was receiving an old age pension preferred to keep quiet about it. There was attached to it a means test as long as your arm and it was somewhat of a stigma to be on the old age pension. But from the day we established the principle of universality, from the day when the right hon. Louis St. Laurent said that even though he did not need it he would go along with universality in taking the pension, it became a mark of honour.

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
We extended this into a good deal of our legislation. In some cases we have developed a double-barreled proposition such as in old age security where the basic amount is universal and the guaranteed income supplement is on a needs test basis. I have had a lot to say about this that is critical, but the fact of the matter is that we have established so much humanity and dignity about old age pensions that Canadians feel a lot happier getting old age security and the guaranteed income supplement than they would if they were getting a form of provincial or municipal welfare. The same is true about the spouse's allowance. It is a form of welfare, but those who get it are getting something that comes from the Department of National Health and Welfare, something which, even though it is not called an old age pension, is related to that pension.
I am trying to impress upon the minister that the words he used when he spoke about the humanity of a program that is already in place were very significant, and I hope he will stand on guard in these studies about our pension programs against those who would destroy or take away the basic element of that humanity, namely, the degree of universality which we have now achieved.
Hear, hear!

I was happy to hear the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent talk about our social programs, and I do not mind his making the reference which is made so often, that the Liberals were in power when most of these bills were brought in. Yes, the Liberals were in power, but some of us were over here all the time, prodding whatever government was over there.
So I welcome the statement that the minister made today about the study, about their concern and about the various problems that need to be considered and, as someone said today about another minister, I am sure his heart is in the right place. However, I hope he will realize that his allies in respect of a good pension program and a good social program are not necessarily those behind him who keep calling for free enterprise, that they are not in the business community that fights against higher pensions and indexation. Some of his best allies are over on this side of the House. He will have our support if he tries to maintain a social program on the basis of the humanity to which he has referred.
Now let me come to what this bill does. The minister left, until the second part of his speech, the part which affects only a few, namely, the change regarding those who are imprisoned. As he said, it affects only 100 persons a year. But I suspect in terms of spouses that it affects very few-half a dozen or a dozen-in the course of a year where the spouse at home is cut off from her spouse's allowance because the old man did something he should not have done and landed in jail. It was inhuman that this situation was there, and I am glad it is being corrected.
The major thing this bill does is to make a change with respect to the position of the spouse in the 60 to 65 age bracket

when the older spouse dies. I know this bill works both ways. The spouse in the 60 to 65 age bracket can be the husband and the older spouse can be the wife, but in 90 per cent or more of the cases it is the other way around. So we are talking about a program which is concerned mainly about women.
The other day when I asked the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) when we would get some legislation implementing our ideas about treating women as persons, he referred to Bill C-6 which was to be brought in today as evidence of the concern of this government for the women of the country. This bill has not moved one inch from the concept which the Privy Council had to reverse 50 years ago. So far as this bill is concerned, women are not yet persons.
Hear, hear!

Women in the 60 to 65 age bracket get a pension or an allowance not because they are persons, not because they are in need. They get a pension on the basis of being able to answer the question: "Have you got a man? Dead or alive, have you got a man?" If they do not have a man, dead or alive, by definition of the bill they do not qualify. But this is being brought in by a government which told us on Persons Day last week that this was to help women.
Let us go back and talk about this legislation. It was first proposed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) in the election campaign of 1974. I remember it very well. I remember being at home that night and hearing on television that he was going to bring in a spouse's allowance which would provide a pension to the younger spouse where the older spouse was over 65 and had a pension. I heard him say on the night he announced it that it would, of course, create some problems, but that it was a step.
Certainly it has created problems. When it was brought in in 1975, coming in effect that fall, it provided that where the spouse between 60 and 65 was married to and living with an older spouse who was on the pension, the younger spouse gets the spouse's allowance, and that it can be in total the equivalent amount of the old age security and the guaranteed income supplement. But the provision of course was that if the older spouse died, then the allowance of the younger spouse was cut off at that very moment. That was corrected earlier this year, when the Liberals were still in power, by extending the allowance six months. Of course, at that time the Tories said, "Why not extend it to age 65?" That is what the government is now doing.
None of these arrangements-the first one, the one for the continuation of six months or the one which now provides for the allowance to be continued to age 65-does anything about the fact that they do not do a thing for a woman between 60 and 65 who is a spinster. Is she not a person just as much as the woman who has a husband, or the widow of a husband who died within the last six months? The bill does not do a thing for the hundreds of widows in the country who were widows before they reached the age of 60. If a woman's husband dies the day the woman is 59 years, 11 months and 29 days old, she does not qualify. She only qualifies if she gets over that point
October 22, 1979

before the husband dies, and only if she can pass the means and needs tests and gets family allowance.
I could talk about the other side of it. The same is true for bachelors and widowers who are left. But statistics show that that is not the problem. The problem is the position of women. Recently we had the report from the National Council of Welfare which underlined how serious the income problem is for older women. When I raised this with the previous minister of national health and welfare, she and her predecessor used to say, "What about those between 55 and 60?" Yes, 1 think they need help too, and I feel very strongly about that. But in this legislation we are talking about a particular age bracket, 60 to 65. In that age bracket we say to women, "You will get help not because you are a woman, not because you are a person, not because you are in need, but on the basis of marital status". It was wrong in its conception in the first place. It should never have been brought in in those terms. Although this fixes it up for 180 persons a month, it does not do away with the fact that all those others out there are not going to get it at all. My answer to this has been made many times and I say it again: We should really have a pension available between 60 and 65 to all persons who are out of the labour market.
Hear, hear!

I welcome the applause for that position, but I note that it is coming from my own colleagues, not from the rest of the House. Much as I feel that that is what it should be,
I could be persuaded into accepting, as a beginning, a pension in the 60 to 65 age bracket to all persons in need. I am a lifelong fighter against means tests and needs tests, but 1 would accept a needs test a thousand times over a marital test. This is inhuman, this is degrading, and this is as antiquated as the Supreme Court decision back in the twenties before the Privy Council turned it over.
I think the minister should really go to work on this. He should not wait until he is able to revise the entire pension program. He should concentrate on the area between 60 and 65. For those over 65 at least we have our universal program, the supplement, health services, senior citizen housing and so on. Things are not rosy for those over 65, but they are a lot better than they were when we started fighting for these things a half century ago. But in the 60 to 65 bracket the position of women is really quite intolerable, and this bill does not touch it. It touches it for 2,200 people. I thought it was 2,400, but 1 accept the minister's statement that it would touch 2,200 people a year. That is 180 persons a month, or six persons a day.
The fact of the matter is that every day in this country six women in the 60 to 65 age bracket who are on the allowance become widows. They are taken care of by this legislation, but all the spinsters in that bracket, all the women who were widowed before they reached 60, or under this bill widowed six months before this bill passes, are not covered at all. Tell us this is a small step, tell us we must vote for it. Of course we
Old Age Security
will, but the minister should not stand up and brag, in light of what he is leaving undone by this bill.
A moment ago I referred to the six-month provision. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) asked an appropriate question just as the minister sat down. I hope something will be done about that when we get into committee.
The bill provides that its terms shall be effective, after it has royal assent, for those who become widows after it has had royal assent or for those who became widows not more than six months before the date of royal assent. That means that if we have passed this bill by the end of October, persons who became widows at the end of April will qualify, but those who became widows in the middle of April do not qualify. If the government switches to the borrowing authority tomorrow, then goes on to the tax bills and does not bring this bill back until some time in November, then those who became widows in the first part of May will not qualify.
That is really a form of blackmail against this House. We were into the bit last session when that six-month clause was being added. Perhaps I was doing some of the blackmailing. I was insisting that the Tories should let that go through because every day we delayed meant another six or seven did not get it. I blamed the Senate for delaying it a day or two as well. Surely that can be fixed up. Surely we can provide that any woman, any person if you want-as I say, the number of men affected in that lower age bracket is not great-who has been on spouse's allowance at all since the program began, and who is still under 65, should have it reinstated under the provisions of this bill. It started in 1974 so we cannot go back all the way, but let us not leave out any widows not yet 65.
I move on to say that I like the minister's four-thirds provision, which is such that the widow who survives will get not just the same amount, the half that she was getting before, but would get an amount based on her income. Surely when the government is doing this it is unthinkable to leave that provision there, because the widows of today whose husbands died five or six months ago will be looking at Parliament and asking how long it is going to take to get this through. There is a deadline in there that is really most unfair and most unkind. I know this, that if the government does that and makes it available to all those who have been on the allowance, I will still be pointing out how unfair that is to all the other widows, and to all spinsters or bachelors, if you like. As long as you have this marital provision in this legislation you are in effect saying that these people do not get their rights, do not get their benefits, because they are persons; they get it on the basis of a marital test, and that just does not make any sense in this day and age at all. I hope that much of the bill will be corrected.
As I say, even if we win that-and we will be glad that we won that little bit so that the number helped will not just be 2,200 in a year but might be a few more-that still does not get away from the fact that we have not yet really done

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
anything about the general need for income maintenance that applies in the 60 to 65 age bracket.
1 note that the draw the other day in respect of private members notices of motions was a fairly good one for me. 1 believe my pension motion is number six, so it will not be very long until we get to that. This is not a new motion. It has been there right along. The only difference is that 1 keep raising the figure as to what the basic old age pension ought to be. This means that when we do get to it I will have an opportunity in another debate to talk about the needs of our older people as a whole.
The minister took some time today to refer to these other matters. I believe the basic amount of old age security must be increased. I believe we have to do something about indexing. 1 was pleased to note, that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) was agreeing outside the House to something I had asked for, namely, a special cost of living index for senior citizens. That formula by which it is always five to eight months behind is not only unfair, it denies all of the modern capacities we have with computers to work things out. You know, Mr. Speaker, it would not take long to devise an index that would give people a pension based on the cost of living in the month they get the cheque instead of a pension based on the cost of living of five to eight months ago.
The Canada Pension Plan needs to be improved in a number of respects. One of the most important respects, and I think it is appropriate for me to speak to it today because supposedly we are talking about women, is the position of women in the home. I know all of the arguments about the Canada Pension Plan being an earnings related pension plan. I was in on the work that led up to the plan and had a good deal to do with the passage of that bill. I accept the basic principle that it is an earnings related plan, but there is no reason in the world why there could not be an equivalent to the Canada Pension Plan for housewives working in the home.
Let me refer back again to last week; women are persons. We decided that 50 years ago, or the Privy Council decided it for us when our own Supreme Court could not see it that way. However, in terms of pension rights the woman who goes out and works in industry, works in the office or works outside the home has certain pension rights which do not apply at all to the woman who does a terribly important piece of work in this country, staying at home raising a family and so on. There are some, of course, who do both.
I noticed with interest that my friend the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) has a motion on the order paper which is fairly high on the list calling for pension rights for women who remain in the home. The other day when we discussed persons and so on, the Prime Minister expressed the hope that it would not take us another 50 years to move as far as we have moved in these last 50 years. A good deal of that rests on the shoulders of this very minister. It is on the shoulders of some other ministers as well. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. McKinnon) has a few reforms he must make. The President of the Treasury Board is responsible for the Public Service Superannuation Act which needs some

reforms as well. The Minister of National Defence has to do with the pensions of retired armed forces persons, and the Solicitor General (Mr. Lawrence) has to do with the pensions of retired members of the RCMP. There is the whole question of what happens to railway pensions and private pensions, but the lead in all of these things has been taken by this department.
Mind you, the old age pension got started in the first place before there was any Department of National Health and Welfare, but that helped to bring on the department and since then the lead in terms of pension humanity, to use the minister's word, has come from the Department of National Health and Welfare. 1 refer to lowering the age, getting rid of the means test, expanding the amount and all these other things our people need. I hope this minister will really get to work on this.
I like the idea of further studies. I have been through a good many of them, and most of the ideas are really there. I do not like the talk about "in the eighties". I know it will be 1980 in two or three months, but "the eighties", that is a decade; that is ten years down the road. Many of these people we are concerned about will not be living then. Some of us intend to go a lot longer than that, but many of them will not be here.
There are some things, such as the indexing bringing it up to date and making it fit the costs the old age pensioners have to meet, covering women for their services in the home and dealing with the problems of widows and veterans and so on, that require attention, and these are things in respect of which action could be taken soon. I hope the minister will get to work on them without delay.
Rather than take the floor again at eight o'clock I shall conclude my remarks now by saying again that I am pleased the minister is in this spot. As I look over the crowd on that side of the House I believe he has probably got as much of a heart as any of them over there. There are many on that side who go the other way, on the basis of the speeches they made last week. I am glad the minister has some changes in mind and I hope he realizes that the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. LeBlanc) and 1 are really supporting him, really backing him up when we say we will surely vote for this bill. But it is such a small step he should not expect us to continue to sing the minister's praises until he deals with these other issues. In terms of what we are talking about today, let us do something fast to treat women in terms of pensions as though they are really persons and not just individuals who get their pensions, in many instances only because of their attachment to a man. Surely that day has gone.
October 22, 1979
