He said: Mr. Speaker, I present this motion to Parliament to initiate a new round of discussion on constitutional reform and, more specifically, discussion on the major first step of this process which is agreement on an amending formula followed
October 22, 1979

by patriation. I trust that in the next round of discussion more debate will occur in the legislatures of this country. This process of constitutional patriation and finding agreement on an amending formula, though almost entirely the preserve of conferences by the first ministers and their subordinates, should begin to move directly into the legislatures and into this Canadian Parliament. Constitutional discussion and decisionmaking has to transcend what has become known as executive federalism.
First of all, I wish to commend the mammoth efforts of the former prime minister and now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) for his initiatives and dedication to constitutional renewal and reform. Indeed, all of the past efforts at constitutional renewal are commendable even in their failure. Though the intent of the previous government was commendable, the comprehensive, two-stage approach of total constitutional renewal proved to be too complex and too encompassing for even the most elementary agreement. It did, however, confirm the former approach of patriation with amending formula, followed by a stepwise renewal. Such an approach was pursued through the decade of the sixties culminating in near success at the constitutional conference of October 14, 1964.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) is to be commended for his wisdom in recognizing the applicability of such an approach when he reached agreement with four premiers at the Kingston conference on September 16, 1977. He said in the communique resulting from that conference:
We are all committed to the objective of bringing the constitution home, so that we can change any part of it without going through the Parliament of the United Kingdom. We are confident that a new Progressive Conservative Prime Minister at Ottawa could bring us both the new attitudes required and the necessary political co-operation among all provincial governments.
Premier Bill Davis of Ontario is recognized as a consistent and strong proponent of patriation as a paramount priority. His consistency is commendable in my estimation.
History condemns us all for failing thus far to patriate the constitution, to find an amending formula and become a whole nation in law and in fact. It was during the federal-provincial conference of 1927 that questions concerning the constitution and its amendment were first debated. The search for an actual amending formula was re-initiated and addressed under the leadership of the former prime minister, the late Right Hon. John Diefcnbaker, in the 1960s. Debates emerging from that period centred on the search for a constitutional amending formula and resulted in the Fulton-Favreau formula in 1964.
At the conclusion of the federal-provincial conference held in Charlottetown on September 1 and 2, 1964, to commemorate the centennial of the conference of the Fathers of Confederation which took place in that city in 1864, the Prime Minister, the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson and the premiers issued a communique. In it, the late prime minister and premiers "affirmed their unanimous decision to conclude the repatriation of the BNA Act without delay". The communique added that they decided to complete a procedure for amending the constitution in Canada based on the draft legislation proposed at the constitutional conference of 1961
Constitutional Amendment
which they accept in principle. The attorneys general of Canada then met to complete the amending formula.
At a conference of Canadian first ministers on October 14, 1964, the first ministers unanimously agreed upon an amending formula. The communique issued by the late Prime Minister Pearson and the premiers from that conference states that when the amending procedure becomes law, all future amendments to Canada's constitution will be made in Canada instead of by the parliament of the United Kingdom. The communique added the following:
As a result our constitution will have become, for the first time in the history of Canada, truly and wholly Canadian.
The text of the bill embodying the amending procedure, "An act to provide for the amendment in Canada of the Constitution of Canada", and unanimously approved by the then prime minister and all the premiers of Canada on October 14, 1964, has been used as the basis for the bill proposed in the motion that is before this House today-almost exactly 15 years later. As there was unanimous provincial agreement at that time, the preamble to this motion states that all provinces have requested and consented to the enactment of such a bill. However, I anticipate that there will be a lot more discussion.
Some changes, of course, were made to accord with the reality of the intervening events of the last 15 years. In particular, clauses 5, 7, 10 and 12 are new and unique. Nevertheless, the basic principles embodied in this motion now before the House may be summarized. Before I summarize the principles, however, I should like to say that there are some provinces that desire more extensive veto power and would argue that the 20 per cent in clause 5 should be reduced to, perhaps, 15 per cent or even 10 per cent. That is a debatable point.
The principles of the bill may be summarized as follows. First, the BNA Act of 1867, with modest amendments, has served this nation well and renewal should be a gradual and stepwise process.
Second, this bill, if passed, would effectively patriate the constitution to Canada and provide a formula for subsequent revision in Canada through parliamentary and legislature approval.
Third, this bill incorporates a constitutional amending formula which (a) requires the unanimous agreement of the legislatures of all provinces as well as the Parliament of Canada to amend existing provincial powers, including natural resource ownership and control and the use of the English and French languages; (b) generally permits the provinces to amend their provincial constitutions as they deem appropriate; (c) generally permits the federal government to amend the constitution on purely federal matters; (d) provides a mechanism for the people of Canada to initiate constitutional amendment; and (e) provides a formula for amending the constitution generally in all other areas, which gives some emphasis to population representation rather than just empha-

October 22, 1979
Constitutional Amendment
sizing provincial legal entities and their equality of status within the federation.
Fourth, it establishes the requirement that no province can unilaterally secede from the federation in total or in part without the unanimous agreement of all the members of the federation.
Fifth, it recognizes the basic right to self-determination of the two linguistic solitudes, English and French, in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, time does not permit me to discuss in depth the implications of the various principles embodied in the amending formula proposed in this motion. Permit me to state, though, that I do not think we should be deterred by the impending Quebec referendum from seeking a way to patriate the Canadian constitution with an agreed upon amending formula. I am of the opinion that Canadians of French origin wish to remain, and will remain, as partners with the rest of us in this Canadian federation, but only through their own willingness resulting from the respect, recognition and advantage they receive from partnership.
The partnership will not endure through force or coercion and the right for self-determination must never be denied but rather held as an unequivocal right within the constitution itself. All parts of this nation form a whole which is unique in history, with a potential to lead the world a century hence, coveted by peoples and governments the world over. Indeed, I was quite surprised to read article XI of the United States articles of confederation. Perhaps 1 could put that on the record, Mr. Speaker. It reads as follows:
Canada acceding to this confederation, and joining in the measures of the United States, shall be admitted into and entitled to all the advantages of this union; but no other colony shall be admitted into the same, unless such admission be agreed to by nine states.
Mr. Speaker, in closing may I say that, having been a provincial MLA, it is my intention to initiate debate on this matter in any way I possibly can in as many provincial legislatures as possible. All elected representatives in Canada must relate positively to constitutional understanding and reform. It is not the exclusive reserve of lawyers, as I have been told on several occasions.
It is also time for us as a nation to cut our apron strings, to become full masters in our own house and, indeed, to become a whole member nation in the community of world nations. It is the way of the future for a great country called Canada.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to speak in this House on the most basic law governing this assembly.

Mr. Speaker, I have to admire the courage of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) in tackling such a subject in what I believe is probably his first address in this House and, in addition to taking on the subject, for offering some new approaches to the older Fulton-Favreau formula.
I noted that he said that we all welcome the day when Canada will have a fully Canadian constitution in the sense that the process of amending, too, will be one which is wholly Canadian. I welcome that statement from the other side of the

House. I hope, however, this is not to be at any price. I hope we are not to feel that we must achieve this Canadian process of amending regardless of the content of the legislation by which it is attained. I submit that might well be a serious mistake.
There are some procedural problems with this motion. I am not going to challenge it on a procedural basis but I think I ought to mention that there are such procedural difficulties. For instance, the formula is not in the usual form for a joint address of this kind. Perhaps, more important, you will note that the words used contain a certain assumption of fact which is not true.
The address reads in part as follows:
Whereas the Parliament of Canada and the legislature of each and every province of Canada have requested, and consented to-
This is an hypothesis contrary to fact. There is no such request in this case and I doubt that there is likely to be. I am willing to go along with the hypothesis, however, and assume that this event has happened and that we are concerned with debating it. In other words, I do not want to go on debating the procedure, but would rather come to the substance. I think, however, that these points should be noted in passing.
Basically the hon. member has presented us with the Fulton-Favreau formula of 1964 with a few changes. In clause 5 he has changed the formula which is used, and rather than providing for a consent formula, he has provided for a rejection formula. Generally speaking, however, the approach is the same as in Fulton-Favreau. However, clauses 7, 10 and 12 are entirely new, as he mentioned. They are additions to the Fulton-Favreau approach. In clause 7, he provides the right of secession for any province, which may be exercised with the consent of all of the provinces and of the Parliament of Canada. In clause 10 he provides for referenda on constitutional matters, and in clause 12, which is the linguistic solitude clause, he also provides for referenda on the basis of linguistic groups.
1 am almost tempted to sit down at this point to allow maximum opportunity for those on the government side to say whether or not they agree with these proposals. It strikes me that the hon. gentleman is being brave indeed in his own ranks in proposing the right of secession. I wonder how many of his colleagues on that side agree with him. There is one member I would like to hear from on that subject whom I see smiling at me. I would mention his constituency if I could remember it. I am told by one of my colleagues it is the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).
It seems to me the provision regarding referenda is directly at odds with the attitude his own government has taken with respect to the referendum bill introduced by the previous government, one which was supported by members on this side for certain kinds of purposes but not in such broad terms as is being proposed here by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko).
October 22, 1979

With respect to clause 12, 1 am not sure that I expect objections to be raised by the other side, but I am certainly prepared to raise one myself. 1 do not like the phrase "two linguistic solitudes". I can only think of the word "solitude ' as implying an enclave, with a lack of communication. If that is sometimes true in Canada, it is not what we would wish to enshrine in our constitution, and surely it is not something that we would want to perpetuate. It is extraordinary that the translation into French of the words "two linguistic solitudes" uses the words "deux groupes linguistiques", which mean something entirely different. They mean two linguistic groups. It takes the sting out of "solitude" by transposing it to a neutral word. The second time the phrase is used in English, speaking about the right of self-determination of each of these solitudes, the French has "de ces deux entites" which means "of these two entities".
I do not intend to charge the hon. member with the quality of the translation. Either the linguistic facilities of the House have let him down or the assistance he has received from his colleagues has not been equal to this occasion. However, it is important to note the difference in flavour between the English and the French on this point. Since the hon. member in his speech, as I caught it, used the phrase "two linguistic solitudes", I think we are entitled to think that it is that notion he wants to get across. I do not know whether members on the other side will object to this phrase, but I profoundly object to this phrase as describing any part of the reality of Canada.
I have said that principally this motion which is before us incorporates the Fulton-Favreau formula. That formula was, it is true, as the hon. member for Edmonton East has pointed out, agreed upon by the first ministers of Canada in 1964. But that agreement was very short-lived. It was an agreement without ratification, if I may put it that way. There was no follow-up. It is very similar to what happened after the agreement at Victoria in 1971. It will be recalled that at that time, when Premier Bourassa returned home-I think he had learned from the previous experience of 1964 that he had to keep his options open and so he did not give a final answer at Victoria-he found public opinion in Quebec was so opposed to the agreement that he was not prepared subsequently to ratify it.
In 1964 the follow-up was not so clear-cut. There were opposition politicians in Quebec who campaigned so effectively against the agreement which had been reached by the first ministers that the first minister of Quebec did not dare to go forward. That is why this agreement never matured into actual constitutional change. The agreement was too temporary to allow the change to take place. Indeed, the fact that within a very few years that agreement could be replaced by the Victoria formula indicates a considerable change of heart on the part of the first ministers.
In fact, the two situations were almost identical. In effect, we had agreement by all the first ministers in Victoria on the amending formula. What we did not have agreement on was the total package. It was not the amending formula in particular that Premier Bourassa finally decided to reject. Although it
Constitutional Amendment
was in a sense the adoption of the amending formula before there had been subsequent reform of the constitution, the objection was not primarily and directly to that clause as such, as I recall it; it was to the totality of the package reached at that time.
We thus have a very similar agreement seven years later which changed, I submit for the better, the provisions of the amending formula which was agreed to in 1964. Why do 1 say that the change was for the better, Mr. Speaker? Because a large part of the rigidity which had been incorporated into the amending formula in 1964 has been removed. The Fulton-Fa-vreau formula, if it had been adopted, would have been the most restrictive amending formula of any federation in the world. In all other countries there is provision for amendment which does not require the unanimous agreement of all of the governments in the country in order to bring about a change.
In the United States there are two kinds of provisions for constitutional amendment. One is through Congress and one through popular vote. In Germany, amendments to the basic law require a two-thirds majority in both Houses, the Bundestag and the Bundesrat. The Lander or the states are not consulted directly but participate through their representatives in the Bundesrat. In Australia, the amending formula requires a change to be adopted by the Australian parliament and then it provides for a referendum by the people in the states-not by the governments of the states, but a reference to the people in the states.
The Fulton-Favreau formula, if one looks at it closely, would, as I have suggested, require unanimous agreement of the governments of Canada in everything that really matters in the British North America Act. Let us just look at the words as they are presented to us by the hon. member for Edmonton East. In clause 2 of the motion which is before us, the operative words are:
No law made under the authority of this part... shall come into force unless it is concurred by the legislatures of all the provinces.
It reads "all the provinces", not some, not a proportion as the Victoria formula would have required, but all the provinces. That applies to the four named categories, the first being "the powers of the legislature of a province to make laws". That is obviously section 92 of the British North America Act. It is by that section that such power is established. Section 92 is the heart of provincial power, along with section 93.
Section 93 is taken care of later in the Fulton-Favreau formula and equally restrictively, but the provisions in section 92 could not be changed without the unanimous consent of the provinces. And so on through the other categories: the rights or privileges granted or secured by the legislature or the government of a province, the assets or property of a province and the use of the English or French languages.
I can hardly argue historically that this is an Alberta amendment, but it clearly is the Alberta position in constitutional negotiations today. It is the position that Premier Lougheed has been putting forward, that there should be unanimous consent by the provinces for any constitutional amendment.

October 22, 1979
Constitutional Amendment
I believe it is based on a profoundly simplistic notion of the constitution. It is based on a belief that if only this could be written into the constitution no further changes could be made. It forgets the fact that the greatest changes in the constitution are those which have been written in by the courts-decisions by the Privy Council and by the Supreme Court.
The notion that conflict could be cured, or the constitution "frozen" as it were, by provisions of this kind ignores the dynamics of the constitution; it ignores the fact that issues arise and that powers overlap, that the power over property and civil rights which is in section 92, and thereby conferred on the provinces, conflicts with almost all the federal powers, the power over trade and commerce, for example. What a court has to do when it is confronted with a situation where either of those rights could apply is to decide which has sway or how far either should be allowed to prevail. That is not a question that can be solved by saying the constitution must not be changed. You do not have to change the constitution by a formal document if a court is going to say that in such and such a case the federal power over trade and commerce is the one that applies and that provincial power over property and civil rights shall not prevail. That is the real question as to the meaning of these powers and it is one which will not even be touched.
Even if the constitution could be frozen, though, the question is whether it should be. Should we freeze our constitution for all time which is, in effect, what we are doing? The reason we have failed to reach agreement in all the many constitutional conferences which have been held is mainly that, though it is not necessary in law, we have been proceeding on the basis that there must be unanimous agreement, on the basis of a political tradition of somewhat short duration that all the provinces have to agree before anything can be done. As long as this is the basis upon which we are proceeding, I feel we will never succeed in arriving at any agreement, that we will never make any progress because there is scarcely a subject upon which all the provinces can be expected to agree.
In recent years in Canada we have seen an enormous growth of provincial power, a dramatic increase in provincial revenues and bureaucracies. Perhaps even more striking is the increase in the provincial self-image, or the self-image of the provincial governments, and particularly of the premiers. These are minor potentates, Mr. Speaker, and sometimes they regard themselves as being much more than that. They have too much power already inasmuch as they have been able to stymie any agreement on changes to the constitution. I, for one, could not accept a constitutional amending formula which would forever give every government the right to stop all progress.
All right is not on one side, Mr. Speaker. We obviously could not accept amendments to the constitution by federal decision alone even though this House is representative of every province. The fact is, of course, that since there is representation by population some areas are better represented, as they should be, than are others. So the provinces must "have a say". But they ought not to be able to have such a say

that every last province has to agree to everything that is done. That, Mr. Speaker, is really the nub of it, whether we ought to freeze our constitution at this time and say, in effect, there will be no further changes or that they can be made only by a process which is so excruciatingly difficult that the process will probably never be accomplished, or whether we ought to adopt something which is more flexible and which allows more room to grow.
I think I can speak for all members in my party-I certainly speak for myself when I say that my vision is one in which there is more flexibility, more openness for the future, more opportunity to grow. It is that model, rather than the polar model, which I recommend to the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko).

Mr. Speaker, first I should like to commend the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) for so early in his tenure as a member of this House bringing forward proposals for the amending structure, new in at least four respects. If we do not manage to pass this measure today-and I think it is unlikely because there are many aspects which give rise to discussion- I hope the hon. member will not be discouraged from pursuing the idea that this Parliament should be engaged much more than in the past in the discussion of constitutional reform, including an amending formula.
I entirely agree with him that over the past 50 years, going back, as I believe he mentioned, to 1927, most of the discussion with regard to the British North America Act took place between the federal government and the provinces; members of Parliament were, by and large, excluded from those discussions, to say nothing, of course, of ordinary citizens. So I commend the hon. member on bringing his proposal forward for four quite substantial changes from the Fulton-Favreau formula and advocating that there should be further and more extensive parliamentary discussion of this subject.
I agree with him, too, that the previous government did make a valiant effort to address the matter, though it did so in too complex a way. Whether or not the present government intends to set up a committee of this House, or perhaps a joint committee with the other place, I do not know. Perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton East knows. In my opinion it would be a good idea. Canada is going through a very serious time. As we all know, the referendum is coming up in Quebec and I believe it would be helpful for us if we were able to address, in a relatively non-partisan way, not only the matter of an amending formula but the direction this country should take, generally.
This brings me to my own feeling that, although the BN A Act has served us very well over the years, the time has come for making changes, if not, indeed, for a new constitution. Therefore I would hope that we would not only be able to patriate the BNA Act but, almost at the same time, that we would be in a position to make very substantial changes in it.
It is a pity we cannot engage in a real debate on this subject, because I have a number of questions to ask the hon. member
October 22, 1979

for Edmonton East about his four new proposals. The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) suggested that clauses 7 and 12 said pretty much the same thing. I do not think I agree. Clause 7, as I read it, says no province may secede from the federation unless the act of secession is approved by Parliament and the legislatures of all the provinces. The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville referred to that as a right of secession. I really do not think it is a right of secession when the act of secession must be approved not only by the federal Parliament but by the legislatures of all the provinces.
More seriously, when you get to clause 12, the hon. member for Edmonton East is in fact giving what he calls linguistic solitudes-1 prefer the word groups-the right to secede without the approval of any of the legislatures, simply through a referendum on the part of the group wishing to secede. I could not support this measure because I see what appears to be an inconsistency between those two clauses, on one hand saying no province can secede without the approval of the Parliament of Canada and every province of Canada, and on the other hand saying of the two major linguistic groups, either one may secede without reference to provincial legislatures or the federal Parliament.
I have already mentioned that the word "solitude" was perhaps not the best to use. I have noted that the French use different words. In French it is really groups or entities. 1 have been wondering, but did not have time to dash out and check, what word was used when Hugh MacLennan's book "Two Solitudes" was translated. Other hon. members may recall.
Solitude.

That is interesting. Then there is a quite substantial difference here in the translation. I am not at all clear on what is meant in the second paragraph of section 12. I do not understand-
-shall occur not along established provincial territorial boundaries but along such contiguous territorial boundaries that are duly and legally negotiated between the two-
Perhaps he can explain it to me later. I am serious in saying 1 hope we will pursue further discussion and debate in this House on the amending formula and on the British North America Act itself.
Clause 10 is another addition to the Fulton-Favreau formula. This is an interesting proposal to initiate constitutional changes through national referenda. 1 was not here, nor was the hon. member, in the last House, but I understand that the Conservatives who were then in opposition opposed the use of referenda. 1 do not know whether the hon. member talked with any of his fellow Conservative members to see what they think of this.
In a country like Australia, which is a relatively homogenous society, there is a lot to be said for the use of referenda in constitutional reform. I am not at all sure that is the case in a country which has a very real duality in linguistic terms.
Constitutional Amendment
Referenda under such circumstances may indeed be divisive. Although he is requiring a 50 per cent plurality of all votes in each and every province, and that would undoubtedly lessen the divisiveness, the chances of getting such a plurality on most of the matters that might be brought forward would be very limited.
It was, however, an interesting proposal. It might have answered to some extent the complaint of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville that the approach suggested in this resolution is not sufficiently flexible. I agree with him that basically this resolution is asking for the unanimous approval of all provinces on anything to do with section 92. Although it has been our practice by and large-not entirely-to have unanimous agreement of all provinces before an amendment is sent to Westminster, nevertheless to entrench this into the amending formula would, I agree, be extremely rigid.
My understanding of clause 10, the referenda clause, is that it tries to develop a little bit of flexibility which is not otherwise there. Although I basically disagree with the use of referenda in a country like Canada, I thought that was an ingenious way to try to get around the problem of unanimous approval of the provinces.
I hope the hon. member realizes that if a referendum did affect property and civil rights, if it were passed and so on, it would mean the provincial legislatures would not be able to veto it. At least that is my understanding of the way he has worded the referendum clause.
On the clause that is now clause 5, I would have thought that on non-critical matters 20 per cent was a reasonable percentage and it really would not need to be any lower. I hope hon. members realize clause 5 does not really touch any of the guts of the British North America Act because it does not touch section 92 at all.
I find I have a sufficient number of questions and puzzlements, particularly on what I see as a conflict between the secession clause, clause 7, and the linguistic groups clause and their rights to secession, clause 12, that I would say the bill needs a good deal of working over before it can go any further.
I want to applaud the hon. member again on suggesting that we should at least start debating some of these issues in this House. Since he has raised this matter, I am particularly interested in knowing whether he has any views about some of the proposals brought forward by the previous government, particularly the House of the Federation proposal of which we in this party were extremely critical. The hon. member will remember this was a proposal to abolish the Senate and create a new body to be called the House of the Federation. I would like to know his views on that, whether he has views not only on an amending formula but on the important substantive changes that we might see in the constitution of Canada. I look forward on some other occasion to debating those matters.

Mr. Speaker, I compliment the hon. member on bringing forward the question of constitutional amendment. It is high time we were able to

October 22, 1979
Constitutional Amendment patriate our constitution. For too long, when speaking to others, Canadians have been embarrassed that we cannot in any way alter our constitution without the permission of Westminster. Elowever, my friend has unfortunately not entirely considered some of the concerns that have been expressed by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) and the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett).
One of the major problems in our country is that the provinces are of various sizes and economic strengths. Prince Edward Island was at one time a pretty good province in Canada in terms of comparative strength, but now has far less economic strength than my city of Mississauga, less than half its population. It is unable, except with enormous assistance from the federal government, to maintain the whole plethora of provincial obligations. To a large extent the same applies in other provinces.
It is impossible for large provinces with economic strength to suggest in any way that some small province, such as perhaps the province of Manitoba or the province of Nova Scotia, should have the right to veto any change in the Constitution of Canada, but indeed that is what the effect of the hon. member's motion would be. What we have to do is to rethink what we mean in terms of provinces when we talk about who should be allowed to vote and what unanimity we need in order to amend the constitution.
A number of persons analysing our constitutional problem have asked, "Why don't we divide Canada into realistic economic regions? Why can't we have an economic region composed of the Atlantic provinces, and why can't we have, for the purposes of provincial responsibilities, for the purpose of an economic base in that area, one jurisdiction?" Perhaps there is no need to amalgamate completely, but certainly in terms of how things are arranged vis-a-vis the rest of Canada, and in amending the constitution, there should be economic regions and no particular province in those regions should have a veto over the whole of Canada.
Clearly the province of Quebec forms an economic region, and so does the province of Ontario. As we proceed west there is no question, in my view, that the province of British Columbia, perhaps together with the Yukon Territory, is becoming an economic region. I should like to see Alberta, the province of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko), treated as an economic region, together with her sister provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In terms of an amending formula we should decide that each economic region should have a veto in amending the constitution if together they cannot agree on it, but that no right of veto in altering the constitution should be allowed to just one province as the provinces now stand.
In going on to other matters I should like to say that the referendum proposal suggested by the hon. member is an interesting one, but when he states that an amendment proposed by referendum must be passed in toto by a plurality of
[Mr. Blenkarn.J
75 per cent, and by at least 50 per cent in any province, then the matter of referendum has to be virtually unanimously agreed to by all voting Canadians. The cost of carrying out such a referendum would then seem like an enormous waste of taxpayers' money. Surely members of Parliament representing their constituencies are well aware when a matter has at least 75 per cent approval and at least 50 per cent approval in the whole of the country. So the referendum proposal, while I think it is interesting and one which perhaps will help us determine whether a particular region will be in favour of an amendment to the constitution, surely deals with a matter which should be considered on the basis of a majority rather than on the basis of 75 per cent approval across Canada and a 50 per cent plurality in every provincial jurisdiction.
The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville and the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam mentioned section 92 of the British North America Act. Surely the proposal will, in some senses, make it impossible to amend the constitution at all. If provincial jurisdictional matters cannot be touched at all without the unanimous consent of ten provinces, then in effect federal jurisdictional matters cannot be touched either, and what you will have done in effect is to have a provision not allowing an amendment ever to be brought to the constitution.
1 bring that to the attention of the hon. member because perhaps this was not his intention.
What concerns me about this proposal is clause 12. In the debate on the Speech from the Throne I spoke last week about my concept of one Canada. This clause refers to two linguistic solitudes, a French Canada and an English Canada, a hyphenated Canadian and different kinds of Canadians. It even goes so far as to suggest that they could break up confederation and go their own way. We have been together in this omelet of confederation since 1867. Our railways have run through each others parts, our canals service each others parts, our investments, our buildings and our enterprises in all of Canada are in English and in French. What we have been trying to do is to break down that solitude so that each one of us can talk to the other.
Surely this party recognizes the separate communities right across Canada. We recognize Canadians whose culture is Italian or whose culture is Indian. What we must do is to treat all Canadians the same in one equal Canada. Any constitutional proposal which, in its very essence, contemplates the breaking up of Canada on linguistic lines, perhaps with new boundaries, as suggested in paragraph 12, is one which 1 and the people whom I represent would be most unhappy to contemplate. I am sure that if the hon. member thought about it he would agree that the people of Alberta also would be most unhappy with it. Surely we have one Canada, and surely we can be one Canadian nation. Surely we cannot all of a sudden try to do the Humpty-Dumpty trick, get all the king's horses and all the king's men together, and put back into two separate packages what is in that frying pan. Sir, we are Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the opportunity to participate in the debate has just
October 22, 1979

about run out. In passing, I want to make two short observations, one in respect of the comments made by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), and the other in respect of the subsequent comments made by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett).
First of all I think that private conversation will bring about a further explanation of paragraph 12 which is quite understandable and which simply addresses itself to the fact that man-made boundaries seldom have much impact on language and culture, and on love and hope.
My other point is addressed to the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville. I wish simply to remind him that the narrowness of his approach to the matter placed before us by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) does not in any way serve the very real point made by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam, that this House should be addressing itself to the nature of this question. For far too long the House has not been seized with this question in a proper and direct way. I commend the hon. member for bringing the matter forward and I hope that at some future date the subject of a bill similar to this will find itself before an appropriate committee of the two Houses of Parliament so that we may enter into a dialogue as members of Parliament perhaps for the first time in this century.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please, the hour provided for private members' business having expired, 1 do now leave the chair until 8 p.m.
At 6 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crombie that Bill C-6, to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to contribute to this debate and to have an opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-6, an act to amend the Old Age Security Act and, more precisely, an act to amend the spouse's allowance. I will keep my remarks relatively brief so as to give as many other hon. members as possible an
Old Age Security
opportunity to express their various views and opinions on this very important and worth-while bill.
Today there are 2.1 million Canadians over the age of 65, approximately 9 per cent of our population. It is estimated that in the year 2001 there will be approximately 3.4 million senior citizens in Canada, representing 11.2 per cent of our population, and by the year 2031 there will be approximately 6.4 million senior citizens representing in excess of 20 per cent of the population.
There is no question that the biggest problem facing many of our senior citizens today is poverty. A single person who receives no other income except that of the basic old age security and the guaranteed income supplement must live off an income of only $3,700 per year, and a couple must live off an income of only $6,800 a year. The result is that one-half of the unattached elderly, and one-fifth of elderly couples, live below the poverty line. This is twice the rate of the general population.
One may ask: what about private pensions? Well, the answer is that private pensions, as they are structured today, are not able to meet adequately the retirement needs of most Canadians. When preparing my notes I was astounded to read that over two-thirds of our elderly do not have private pensions and that almost 60 per cent of working Canadians are not covered by company pension plans. Also it is a fact that very few pension plans are indexed against inflation, and that most of these pensions do not even provide for survivors' benefits.
In view of these very serious shortcomings and inequities in our pension system, particularly as they relate to our elderly, the problem is further compounded for those spouses whose only income is the old age pension and supplement to support his or her spouse who, because that particular spouse had not yet attained the age of 65, is not eligible for old age security, and consequently both spouses are forced to live-or perhaps a better word is survive-on the inadequacy of one pension.
This very serious problem was finally recognized by the government in 1975 with the passage of Bill C-62, the spouse's allowance. Although the bill was commendable in itself and it provided serious relief to the many pensioners concerned, it did not go far enough and some serious inequities still remain. Bill C-62 did not ensure that widows and widowers would be protected in the event of a spouse's death until the survivor became eligible for regular old age security at age 65. Also under Bill C-62 spouses receiving the spouse's allowance lost it if their spouse received a jail sentence of 90 days or more, and payment only resumed when the prison term was served. Although few people are affected by this provision, its application has been the source of inequities in that old age security pensioners face double punishment for their crimes: loss of benefits and imprisonment.
There is no question that it would be considered cruel and inhumane by every compassionate Canadian to have to say that on the death of the older spouse the pension of the younger spouse is terminated after six months. Yet this is the case today. It is a shocking situation that a widow, in her distressing time of sorrow, should receive information that the

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
pension she has been receiving will be cut soon. How is she supposed to live with no pension income? The bereaved spouse is advised, when notified of the termination of the allowance, to apply for provincial welfare, but until application is made and approved several weeks may elapse in which time ordinary living expenses still go on and on and on. Also she is advised to apply for Canada Pension Plan survivor's benefits.
If the deceased partner had been eligible to receive Canada Pension Plan benefits, the widow would have been eligible to receive approximately 65 per cent of the pension her husband received. However, this does not come automatically. Application for survivor's benefits first must be made, and it all takes precious time. To compound the matter further, for widows in Ontario another irony exists inasmuch as she is no longer covered by OHIP, the Ontario Health Insurance Plan. While her husband who was over 65 was living, she was covered as his dependent under the free health insurance provided. Now she must apply for OHIP, and while premium assistance is ultimately available to those eligible, premium payments must be made until the application showing proof of need is approved. This is a very unjust situation when pension income has been terminated.
When Bill C-6 is passed into law it will negate some of the inequities of the present act. Spouse's allowance recipients whose spouses die will continue to receive the allowance until they themselves turn 65 and qualify for old age security in their own right, or until they remarry or die. The second amendment will remove the provision whereby old age security benefits are suspended when an old age pensioner is sentenced to prison for more than 90 days. This also meant that spouses of prisoners entitled to the spouse's allowance lost their benefits as well. The two amendments will benefit more than 2,200 persons in the 1980-81 fiscal year and will cost approximately $4.6 million a year.
While these amendments will alleviate two serious problems, they represent only a further small step forward in relation to the pension system in Canada and the possibilities which still remain for even much greater improvement. No doubt as the Canadian pension system is being continually revised for further improvements, some issues can and will be dealt with quickly, while others more complex will require more time to accomplish.
If I have any criticism at all about Bill C-6 it is the fact that this bill will not benefit those spouses of pensioners who will have been deceased more than six months from the time Bill C-6 receives Royal Assent and becomes law. In other words, the retroactiveness of this bill is very limited, indeed. How was this figure of six months arrived at; why six months, and why not a year or two years? Why not include all eligible widows or widowers?
I have no doubt that Bill C-6 is commendable in redressing some of the glaring inequities connected with the spouse's allowance, but surely we can afford to be a little more magnanimous and extend the spouse's allowance to all widows and

widowers eligible for the allowance, and who are between age 60 and 65, until they themselves are eligible for old age security at 65. Surely this is not only fair but also just.
Therefore it is of the utmost importance that when Bill C-6 is brought before the committee concerned, the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, a change must be sought to have it amended to include the changes I have suggested. The extra cost would be negligible compared to the long over due and much needed benefits that would be received by those concerned who find themselves today living below the poverty line.

Mr. Speaker, I should like for a few minutes to participate in the debate on Bill C-6, and more particularly the first part that guarantees to people between 60 and 65 who receive the spouse's allowance following the death of the other spouse, whether they be widows or widowers, that the benefit will continue to be paid as long as the financial need is there.
I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie) on his first bill, a bill designed to help needy and underprivileged Canadians, and as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, we hope it is a step in the right direction.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the principle of Bill C-6 and it is not my intention to oppose it, and I do not believe my Liberal colleagues intend to oppose this bill either. Unfortunately, the government did not go far enough. It is all very well to say this government is doing more now than the previous government by doing away with the additional six-month period and adding a six-month retroactive effect. If we are serious about doing something, I believe, Mr. Speaker, the government should go a little further so that this measure will apply in all cases of death prior to the legislation rather than future deaths to come or deaths that occur six months before the legislation is implemented. One could ask: why did the previous government not do it? The answer to this, Mr. Speaker, is that it was the intention of the former government to forget all that and replace this survivor's allowance with a guaranteed minimum income program for all people between 60 and 65.
Oh, come on!
The Liberal party at its convention held in Montreal last week, that is this past weekend-
Is that the best you can do?
If he wants to disturb me, that does not bother me at all.
Come on, there.

So the Liberal party this past weekend passed a resolution incorporating the principle of a guaranteed
October 22, 1979

minimum income for anyone between 60 and 65 regardless of marital status, that is whether that person is a widow or widower, single or divorced, but between 60 and 65. The minister felt that the total cost of benefits paid to spouse allowance recipients as a result of that amendment would increase by $400,000 in 1979-80 and $4.3 million in 1980-81. This is not quite accurate since the federal government pays 50 per cent of the welfare benefits given out by provincial governments. The provincial governments will not claim the part of the welfare payments granted to widowers and widows between 60 and 65 who had applied for it. In my opinion this will therefore mean a reduction in the claims of the provincial governments of between $1.5 and $1.7 million. It would therefore be more accurate to talk about a real expenditure of between $2.3 and $2.5 million for the federal government.
In its electoral campaign, the Progressive Conservative government did promise that it would take care of older people. As I said earlier, $4 million may appear in the books as expenditures under Bill C-6 but in fact $2.3 million will be paid in direct assistance. Yet the federal government will spend $2.3 billion for its famous mortgage interest deduction program while everyone knows-and it is a sad fact that the Progressive Conservative members are the only ones who refuse to admit this-that the great majority of older people no longer have a mortgage on their houses.
We often hear about this famous program, Mr. Speaker. We have said often and we will go on saying that this program is discriminatory since older people in general will not benefit from the mortgage interest deduction.
Unfortunately, I must say that Bill C-6 is also discriminatory since it will apply only to spouses and not to single or divorced people.
Mr. Speaker, the minister estimates that more than 2,200 people will benefit from this measure during the current fiscal year, and I can only hope that this will not be to the detriment of other Canadians.

We hope it is a step in the right direction.
This is what worries me, Mr. Speaker. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) has declared many times that he would cut jobs, cut expenses, with no increase whatever in expenditures. With such a policy, and I have asked this during my campaign and during my maiden speech, with decisions and declarations made without studying the consequences, who will suffer among those included in the budget for social welfare as a result of this increase of $2.3 million or $4 million? This money has to come from somewhere. Will the President of the Treasury Board ask the minister to cut some of the family allowances? Will he ask the minister to reduce benefits under the UIC? Will the President of the Treasury Board ask the minister to cut his budget for medicare? A lot of other questions could be asked about this matter, and a lot of questions remain to be answered. Where will the cuts be? Will the minister answer that?

This bill is such a tiny parcel, and represents such a tiny portion of the total budget. I trust the minister will not consider this bill as the great social reform of the Conservative government.
