speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who has spoken often in this chamber and, indeed, across this country on the plight of elderly women and the poverty in which too many of them live,
I am pleased that my first remarks in this chamber as a member of the government are in support of a bill which will go a long way toward removing the discriminatory aspects of the spouse's allowance legislation.
It has been a long fight, and my interest in it has been shared by many members, notably, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I think that he and I have received more letters on this subject than all other members of Parliament. I am sure that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is saying that he only heard from women on the matter, whereas I told him on one occasion that I had received letters from several men who had been left in that particular circumstance as well.
That is what I was saying. I get them from the widows; you get them from the widowers.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He is absolutely right. I endorse that.
This bill is not a minor piece of housekeeping legislation that we should easily gloss over. To me this bill symbolizes the compassion, the common sense, and the instinct for justice and individual dignity that we, as members, must have. I am proud to be associated with this bill, but even more so, with a government that so early in its mandate has moved to eliminate one of the lingering injustices in our pension system. How different was the attitude of the previous government.
This particular bill should have been enacted many years ago. By failing to act, the previous Liberal government caused untold hardship among those least able to protect themselves, widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 65. The origin of that hardship goes back to Bill C-62 of the Thirtieth Parliament, debated in the spring of 1975. I said then, and have said many times since, that certain provisions of that bill were conceived in a spirit of meanness and callousness. Here we had a piece of legislation which enabled the younger spouse of an old age pensioner to receive old age security, on the basis of need, between 60 and 65 years of age. But then what? As

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
soon as the older spouse died, the younger partner lost not only her husband but her pension as well.

The reactionary approach of the former government regarding older women was evidenced in the legislation on spouse's allowance which was tabled in 1975. 1 clearly remember the remarks I made to the then minister of national health and welfare when he appeared before the committee. 1 asked him, among other things, what he and his government had against widows. What really irked us was that the younger spouse who received regular allowance cheques was faced, upon the death of her spouse, not only with the loss of a loved one but also with an immediate stoppage in her allowance. By arguing for the suspension of payments, the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) gave a very clear idea of his government's attitude towards women, in particular, older women. The bill we have before us today, Mr. Speaker, will right this wrong. [English]
The victims of such action have overwhelmingly been women. Statistics have shown that in 90 per cent of marriages the younger spouse is female and that females live longer than males. These women, who in their younger years remained in the home looking after children, with no access to continuing income or pension plans, are the same women who in their later years too often become the victims of a society which has not yet come to terms with equality in the work place.
While women have been "persons" for 50 years, society continues to discriminate against them, and the elderly woman is doubly prejudiced. It was all too easy for the previous government, in the name of saving a few dollars, to have denied and opposed the repeated attempts by my party and the NDP to correct the discriminatory aspects of the spouse's allowance program.
The sums involved have never been great.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, 1 would say to the hon. member in the opposition that the sums involved were never large and the victims were not many but the government of that day would not pay attention. Moreover, this group is anything but highly organized with all the means of professional lobbyists. It is estimated that each month roughly 200 recipients of spouse's allowance have their benefits cancelled. In a full year of operation, the extension proposed today will cost the treasury only $4.5 million. It is not much when human dignity and justice demand it.
I want to take this occasion to salute the many women and, indeed, the men who have insisted, by their letters and their pleas, that this legislation be changed. No issue has so consistently dominated my correspondence or gripped my conscience as the shortcomings of the spouse's allowance.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member in the official opposition laughs about this sort of thing, but 1 can tell him that there are many elderly women in this country who have had cause for tears because of this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: It is not a laughing matter, and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) should know better.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What these women have done by continuing their efforts in letter writing and in representations has been a real exercise in grassroots politics-the efforts, disorganized though they might have been, of the elderly, the poor and the destitute who have been subjected to the callous and frustrating treatment of a government that chose not to listen. The great thing about it is that these people never gave up. In their own quiet and persistent way they knew that common sense and fair play would prevail, even if it took an election and a new government to realize it.
One of these persons was a widow from British Columbia who wrote to me just recently. She enclosed an earlier letter I had sent her in which I had pledged myself to press for the continuation of the spouse's allowance after the death of the older partner. The lady did not have an organization to protect her economic interests. She did not have a lobbyist in Ottawa. She probably did not have a degree in political science or law, but I can tell you she knew where common sense lay, and she is now calling on the government to respond. The support and active encouragement of people such as this widow from British Columbia, regarding the spouse's allowance, is the democratic system working at its best.
This bill removes one inequity, Mr. Speaker. It does not profess to tackle all of the discrimination and injustice that has been allowed to become encrusted in our pension system. Too many of the elderly people who built our schools, our bridges, our roads, and reared our children-too many are living their last years in poverty. And of these poor, it is the women who are the poorest. As the recent study on women and poverty undertaken by the National Welfare Council states:
Most Canadian women become poor at some point in their lives. Their poverty is rarely the result of controllable circumstances, and it is seldom the outcome of extraordinary misfortune. In most cases, women are poor because poverty is a natural consequence of the role they are still expected to play in our society.
The report goes on to conclude:
In our study of low income women in Canada, we found that old women, and especially widows, are more likely to experience poverty than any other group in this country. After a lifetime spent taking care of their spouses and children, these women who had no opportunity to become financially self-sufficient are now abandoned by the generation that benefited most from their work.
That, sir, is an analysis of the plight of elderly women in Canada today. I am delighted that the attitude this government displayed in moving so quickly to extend the spouse's allowance has led us to take two further steps on this difficult road to end poverty among and discrimination against women.
October 22, 1979

[ Translation]
First, the minister responsible for the status of women is currently working with his colleagues on the establishment of an employment strategy for women. That program will tackle the immediate problems women have to face on the job market and, in the longer run, will alleviate the disproportionate burden older women must bear.
Second, as was announced in the Speech from the Throne, a standing committee of Parliament will soon examine the question of financial needs of pensioners in the eighties. 1 hope that those who will be affected by the conclusions of that study will express their points of view as persistently as and even more vigorously than all those who contributed to maintain the spouse's allowance. I urge hon. members who will be involved in this study to come to grips with the problem of the inequalities which still exist in our pension plan and to consider the sensitive questions relating to those Canadians who are not protected by the present laws. What happens to single people, divorced couples, and those who have recently lost their spouses? That question will obsess us as long as women will not be equal partners in the labour force and will not enjoy equal access to pension and old age security plans.
[English)
This bill, sir, is both real and symbolic. It is real in that it corrects an inequity. It is symbolic in that it demonstrates that this government will tackle the problems of the elderly poor with vigour and with compassion. Only through this process can we achieve a humane, sensible, and broadly-based public policy capable of meeting the needs of Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker,
1 am pleased to be able to support this bill. I should like to congratulate, first of all, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), as I know she has fought many many years to have this inequity reversed. I hope that when the bill has passed through committee many of the changes will have taken place, as 1 think we still have many inequities. Certainly some of the people who have been writing to her, and for whom she has been crusading over the last few years, will not be re-instated, as the bill only goes back six months. I am sure the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands will appreciate that. Certainly the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) indicated that he would like to see that changed in committee. We would like to see that changed, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated that his party would as well. I think there is a mood to make the change to ensure that those who have drawn this in the past will be re-instated.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie) on his new job and let him know there is a mood on this side of the House to support him. I know he will run into a good deal of difficulty because of the government's disposition to cut back, to privatize and turn things back to the provinces. This is going to make his job very
Old Age Security
difficult. His job will also be difficult because I get the impression, as do many members on this side of the House, that his department has been downgraded to some kind of a post office arrangement-that the power that was formerly in that department has given to some kind of committee with a super minister of social development. At this point we do not quite know to whom to put our questions as we are not sure who is responsible in the inner cabinet which makes the decisions on what happens in respect to health and welfare. About one quarter of all government expenditures are made through this department.
We will stand behind this minister. I think he is doing his best, and he will have a lot of support for measures of this kind. 1 am also pleased that the minister has instituted a pension review. I hope this review will make things better, although it was indicated by another minister who held a job which does not exist any more, that there was some question whether old age pensions should continue to be universal. 1 do not know whether this is the case, but we keep hearing such things. Someone makes a statement that universality is at stake, or that we have to look at universality because we cannot afford to keep doing what we are doing.
I am not sure whether at this point the government is sending up a lot of trial balloons. Last week the press was writing about gasoline costing $1.45 per gallon, but at the weekend they were writing about gasoline coming down to about a dollar or $1.20 per gallon. The press reported that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) had a meeting in Calgary with the minister from Alberta and they talked about a different price range. The minister has said that he did not have a meeting with that minister in Calgary, but then we found out that he had the meeting in Saskatoon. This type of thing goes on and on, Mr. Speaker.
1 get the feeling that the government thinks it can frighten people with talk of $1.45 per gallon for gas and then those same people will think they are on a good thing when the government starts talking about $1.20 per gallon. I feel that is exactly what has happened with the talk about pensions. Is it a trial balloon for the press? As an example, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), or his office, gave the press the idea that there would be a cut of $1.5 billion in social services, or in the whole area known as social development. This would cover unemployment insurance, social welfare, medicare, pensions-the whole area that would fall under one particular super minister. I asked him a question today and he said that that rumour was certainly not true. Unfortunately, I was not able to ascertain what the cut was going to be, but we keep hearing about a cut. It may be the same kind of cut. We may start with $1.5 billion, then everyone says that we cannot have that. If we end up with a cut of a billion, everybody says that that is much better, it is $500 billion less. It is this kind of thing that I think is going on.
I am not sure whether this government is doing this deliberately, so that when the axe falls it will look benevolent, or
478

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
whether it is accidental. I do not know if it can mount a conspiracy of this kind. Conspiracy takes a lot of thinking. Brains are needed to mount a conspiracy. Perhaps this is giving too much credit where it is not due. But, I am not sure, and I am concerned.
I am concerned when we talk about universality of pensions. If pensions are to be cut back, and people are told that the old age pension-the pension that you and I and my constituents have been counting on for the last 20 years, counting on getting when we are 65-is not going to be there any more, then plans people have made will be for naught. People plan that this security will be available.
I am very disturbed when I hear ministers make this vague reference about universality. I am very disturbed when I hear there are debates taking place around the country on universality. I think this whole area of social security has a formidable principle, that is, universality and extra assistance where needed. These are the two cardinal principles to all of these things.
Universality in medicare, is another example. Are we getting to a point where that is going? I do not know. I really hope it is only that "trial balloon" that I am talking about, that the government is playing some kind of game and that it will get out of that when it is a little older. After all, we are not very good in opposition either. It takes a while to get used to these parts. I am most concerned that at some particular point somebody is going to pop this one on us. Somebody is going to say that we are going to get rid of universality. This is the beginning of this particular debate.
I wish this bill was going further. At times I was embarrassed by the fact that we did not make this move that the government is making today. I think that move could easily have been made, but there was a reason. We wanted to move into a guaranteed kind of annual wage situation, certainly for those people over 60. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre-
It is Winnipeg North Centre.

Winnipeg North Centre, I am sorry. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated, and I agree with him, he would like to see that we return to the age of 60 as being a flexible age by which people can move out of the working force. In the long run this makes a great deal of sense. I believe that if you free people from their jobs at that point, those who want voluntarily to be free, a lot of job openings would be created and there would be a considerable saving at the other end, that is in UIC.
I think we should be moving into an area with some kind of guaranteed annual wage which would permit people to retire at an earlier age if they are not well-or for any other reason. If they need support, this would give them some support. The reason that we steer away from this kind of thinking is that it is too costly and we cannot afford it. The NDP steers toward it but, never having been in power nationally, it has never had to face up to the other side. This is the reason that I am not a member of the NDP, because at some particular point one has

to face up to paying. When we talk about moving in these directions, earlier retirements, extending programs, a complete medicare program-which is costly-we have to spend some time talking about how we raise the money. Certainly when the government is faced with a deficit of $11 billion, $12 billion or $13 billion in a year, there is a grave problem facing it.
We should look at how we got into this situation. Inevitably the Canadian people think that we got into it because we had too many social programs, that too much was being paid out for this, for that, and for the other thing, to name a few, medicare, welfare, pensions for people who have needs, and so on. They think it is because of these programs the government is in a deficit situation. I think that is wrong. It is wrong to make that simple an assumption.
If we take a look at the revenue curves of the past government through the years up to about 1974, 1975, hon. members will find that the revenue and expenditure curves rise at roughly the same rate. One goes up a little more than the other in one year, but the next year it is reversed. But all of a sudden we got into some very significant increase in revenue when we indexed. This is something that we had to do because of inflation. As this government is now finding out, inflation is not a local phenomenom but a world problem. We indexed some things, but then we did something that got us into a lot of trouble. We indexed exemptions on income tax and a whole series of other things which became known as tax expenditures. So the expenditure curve went up this way, and the revenue curve went out like that. If one looks at those curves one can almost find the day and the hour when we indexed exemptions in income tax.
If this government wants to continue some of these programs and give the people the kind of social security that Canadians can expect-because we are a wealthy country in many ways-some of these tax expenditures will have to be examined. There are a whole series of them. The National Council on Welfare in a book written in 1977, I believe, called "The Hidden Welfare System Revisited", mentioned the year 1975 to 1976. This was the last year that figures were available. In that book it indicated that the tax expenditures increased by 17.9 per cent that year and government expenditures increased by only 10.4 per cent. Basically there was about a 27 per cent spread there. These things will have to be examined.
When exemptions are indexed to the cost of living, which is a desirable thing-there is no question about that-each year one has to add to the exemption created in the last year. For example, if it is $1.5 billion this year, over four years it is probably $5 billion a year that we are talking about. This is another area about which we should think seriously. I would hope that this minister, even though he may be in a somewhat lower echelon than the Minister of National Health and Welfare should be, will be elevated to the inner circle. Also I hope, before cutting back on these programs we can begin to start paying for them by increased taxation of some sort or other, and we should look at some of those tax exemptions.
October 22, 1979

They may have been justified for a short period of time but they are not justified now. We should try to pay for these particular types of programs because they are real programs for people with real problems.

Mr. Speaker, 1, too, would like to congratulate the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Mr. Crombie) on his new post. A minister who comes from cabbagetown can't be all bad. 1 hope his reputation for encouraging citizen involvement at grass roots will extend to his new ministry as well.
My party and I face a dilemma with regard to Bill C-6 in that we must support a bill that we oppose. We must support this bill because we know that 180 people will benefit from it each month, widowed people who need a pension very badly. Therefore, we want no delay. At the same time we are opposed to this bill for two reasons-first, it is based on sexist principles, or, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre said this afternoon, a spouse has to be dependent upon having a man, alive or dead. Second, it does not go far enough to protect those aged 60 or over.
As my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre pointed out this afternoon, it is particularly ironical that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the minister of health should hold up this bill as a celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of recognizing women as persons. In my opinion Bill C-6 is based on an out-dated attitude that Emily Murphy and her colleagues abhored. It denies the basic right of women to be treated and respected as individuals in their own right, entitled to pensions equal to men's regardless of age or marital status. Also, it ignores single, divorced, and separated women, and those who live common law, making them third class citizens with no right to a pension at all until they qualify for an old age pension.
We agree that widows, and widowers too, should have an adequate pension adjusted to their income. As other hon. members have pointed out, the National Council on Welfare reports that one widow in four can expect not to benefit from the employer of her dead husband, and 45 per cent of all widows in the 55 to 64 age group are poor.
Many women who become widows before 65 have worked as homemakers for perhaps 40 or more years. In their earlier years they probably worked 12 hours a day, seven days a week, and all this without pay. After their children had grown up they found they had few marketable skills so they were unable to seek employment in today's market. Unlike working men, they are not entitled to the Canada Pension. Surely these women are entitled to an adequate pension at age 60, or earlier, if one is needed, regardless of whether they are widowed or whether they are legally married.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister of health will take action now to prevent the need for spouse's pensions in the future. The former member for Vancouver-Kingsway, Grace Mac-Innis, strongly advocated that we needed pay for homemakers, and also pensions for homemakers. She recognized that home-
Ol d Age Security
makers should be entitled to equal pay for work of equal value, with a full Canada Pension when the time came for retirement. What work is more valuable to society than child care and home making? Why shouldn't it be recognized as an essential job worthy of pay? Even our kids get allowances for helping in the home these days.
1 cannot stress too strongly that Bill C-6, while necessary as an intermediate step, treats women, and widows particularly, as inferiors, while ignoring many other woman. Eligibility is based on a dependency relationship to a spouse; it treats the woman as an aging sex symbol rather than treating her with dignity as an independent person with rights in her own name. An even greater injustice in this bill is the fact that it completely ignores the needs of single, separated or divorced people who have no other source of income. Again, the majority of these people are women in the 60-65 age group.
More than 50 per cent of the women between 55 and 65 earn less than $4,000 a year, compared to 11 per cent of men in this age group. So we find that single, poor women under 65 are the most deprived group in our society. Many of them live as lonely outcasts in substandard rented rooms. They are not eligible to get into public housing. Many of them have a high incidence of mental health problems and physical health problems, as a result. They live on fixed welfare incomes of less than $200, in British Columbia at any rate, and the cost of living is going up every day. Such single, poor women, and also 11 per cent of single, poor men, have just as much right to an adequate pension as widowed spouses who at least may have a home. I resent having to categorize people in this way.
Band-aid token programs for a very small segment of our society cost a great deal and benefit very few. Bureaucratic welfare programs should be replaced by a social insurance system for those in need. We must aim at an adequate guaranteed income, or perhaps the term "social insurance" is better these days, with cost of living adjustments for all those who cannot afford to work, who are unable to work. As a first step, of course, the target group should be elderly citizens aged 60 and over who have contributed so much to Canada, and who deserve a life free from financial worries. Social insurance should be their right, just as old age pensions are. I should like to point out that in British Columbia during the golden years of 1972 to 1975-
Hear, hear!

-we could afford this. We had a "min-come" program which was introduced for all unemployed persons aged 60 to 65. This program was paid for-and I hope members on the government side are listening to this-from the profits of the British Columbia Petroleum Corporation, which was B.C.'s version of PetroCan. Incidentally, "min-come" was so universally popular that it is being continued by the British Columbia Social Credit government. So it can be done, and I would say the profits of PetroCan might go a long way toward paying the costs of a federal "mincome" program, if we had sense enough to keep it and develop our oil resources.

October 22, 1979
Old Age Security
In conclusion, let me suggest the following priorities. First, let us approve Bill C-6 making it retroactive to include all eligible spouses whether legally married nor not. Second, let us begin now to initiate a "mincome" quaranteed income program, with a COLA clause, for all unemployed persons aged 60 or over. Finally, I say this to the minister, let us plan to set up a guaranteed income system to replace our obsolete welfare system by 1985.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate which has been taking place for many years during each Parliament because, particularly when it comes to the elderly, our social policy is indeed found wanting. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) indicated in her speech a while ago that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and his party have always participated actively in debates on underprivileged people and I congratulate them for doing so. But I want to insist on the fact that the minister, voluntarily or not, did not allude to the very active part that my party and myself have always played on such issues as retirement at 60 and the guaranteed annual income. I suggested many times the idea of optional retirement at 60 and I defended the interests of those who live in poor conditions. I shall come back to that later.
First, Mr. Speaker, we must commend the introduction of this bill by the government. I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie) for having introduced this bill among the first legislative measures to be considered by the House.
I should like to remind the House that as soon as the spouse's allowance was introduced, 1 pointed out the problems raised by the death of the spouse and by the withdrawal of the allowance from the surviving spouse. In March, 1977, I moved a motion under Standing Order 43 asking the government to pay at least two-thirds of the allowance to the surviving spouse. The House is surely aware that quite a number of older persons are faced with acute survival problems. Those people are found especially in the 60 to 65 age bracket. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, employers no longer want to hire those in that age group at a time when they are unable to work because of ill health, and their only financial resort in many cases is social welfare. It is a sad end to have to make do with a small welfare cheque each month after a lifetime of work.
Bill C-6 will be welcomed by senior citizens who were deprived of their allowances. I hope, as they do, that the bill is only a step towards an old age security program at the age of 60. Last year, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, now Secretary of State for External Affairs, brought forward an opposition motion on the same subject as the present bill. The former government did not budge. I am happy the present government did not make only crazy promises during the campaign. This bill, as I said before, is not an end in itself but

a step towards lowering pensionable age to 60. At least, I hope so. The problem goes beyond that.
The economic situation of our pensioners is precarious. Statistics Canada figures that 43 per cent of those who live below the poverty line are people who live alone. Most of them are old people. Pensioners without investment income have no protection against contingencies. Where the constant rise in the cost of living is concerned, they only have the quarterly indexation to help them. That is why, at the time of the debate initiated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs last year, I suggested a plan providing voluntary retirement at 60, a plan to be implemented progressively by lowering retirement age to 60 and making retirement voluntary. In other words, those who can work and want to do so could in fact keep on working. Besides, a study by the department of psychology at Western University, prepared for the national symposium on aging, held here in Ottawa on October 25, 1978, indicated a clear tendency towards early retirement at 60. We would therefore not be imposing early retirement since most of the aged would dearly love to retire sooner.
In Canada at the present time, there are over 2 million pensioners, half of whom receive the guaranteed income supplement. Last year, that old age and guaranteed income supplement program cost the treasury $4.3 billion. There is no doubt that a retirement plan stipulating voluntary retirement at 60, even if it were to be implemented progressively, would cost at the outset considerably more. On the other hand, such a plan would in fact free a number of jobs estimated at something like 287,000 in 1977. That is to say then that opening up those jobs would save considerable amounts in unemployment insurance. It therefore boils down to reorganizing financial outlays within the existing framework. Over the short term, it would mean considerable outlays. But over the medium and long terms, society as a whole would benefit greatly.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that outside the framework of a guaranteed annual income it is difficult to propose final and global solutions. Referring back to the meeting of the welfare council held last fall, I would like to quote from a report submitted by Queen's University which stated:
Adequate revenue, decent housing and means of transport are essential not only for senior citizens but for all citizens.
This quotation shows the merits of a guaranteed annual income system of which we, of the Social Credit Party, have been the most ardent champions since the beginning of our movement. Until now, old age security benefits have fallen short of ensuring peaceful retirement to our senior citizens. They are faced with many problems, from the deterioration of their health to their isolation from the rest of society.
We no longer live in an era when a citizen could some day pretend to enjoy his retirement. What is in store for the elderly is uncertainty and even poverty in certain cases. Therefore we must look far beyond the measures that have been proposed to
October 22, 1979

us today because any program designed to improve the living conditions of the elderly will be without positive impact if it does not get translated into adequate revenue and guaranteed financial security.
Our population is aging which means that because of a declining birthrate and the greater availability of health services, the elderly will make up a growing segment of the Canadian society. It is therefore now that we must prepare to face this situation. We should not wait until that time has come before we react. Some day elderly people will be in a position to organize and ask for their fair share of the riches which belong to them. Future generations of elderly people will have experienced affluence and education. These people will not tolerate as easily their regression into poverty.
The logical solution to the problems which will arise in the future is undoubtedly a guaranteed annual income. In January, 1977, I made the same representations that were listed in my speech today to the then minister of national health and welfare who is now sitting in the opposition side of the House as the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde). The minister told me in his letter dated February 9, 1977, that it was impossible to bring any over-all solution to the problems faced by senior citizens, and that the problems plaguing the disadvantaged and the senior citizens could be resolved to a large extent through the implementation of a guaranteed annual income plan, a program which could be ushered in with the provinces, as had already been done for hospital insurance and medicare plans.
Therefore, it is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will consider very seriously that most important proposal concerning the guaranteed annual income in order to respect the right of all Canadians to a decent standard of living.

Hear hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 will not speak long because 1 think it is in everybody's interest to have the bill voted on and passed this evening, but 1 should like to add a few remarks to the debate. Having listened to the previous Liberal speaker, we can begin to understand why the Liberal party was defeated, although he made serious points as well. We seem to have a little social progress in the country every time we change government, and if there is a minority government, we have a little more social progress. Old Age Security
will not be covered by it, as well as those who became widows more than six months ago. These are all shortcomings. There are not only shortcomings in this bill, there is a whole range of shortcomings in the entire area of social security in this country. This is something for which both the Liberals and Conservatives must take responsibility.
When I started compaigning, knocking on doors in my constituency, I was amazed at the number of elderly people living close to total economic and social insecurity. These are the people who worked hard all their lives, the people who settled and developed the prairies, the people who had to struggle against the severe elements, breaking open the prairies and getting development started. Many of them worked for 25 cents and up to $1 a day, yet saved money. These people were really committed to the work ethic. They have now retired and have seen the system and inflation rob them of their savings. These are the people who live from month to month with total economic insecurity.
It is our system that has produced this situation, and it is the system that has robbed these people of the wealth in this country that they produced in their lifetime. Therefore it is the system surely that must be blamed, and it is a system that members of both the Conservative and Liberal parties continue to support and perpetuate. It is a system in which most of the wealth leaves the country so that the little that remains has to be distributed among our elderly people.
That is nonsense.

An hon. member opposite says it is nonsense. Surely this is a rich country. Everybody agrees with that. Everybody agrees that this is one of the wealthiest countries in the world, with one of the smallest populations in terms of area and resources. That being the case, why is it that we have elderly people trying to live on $200 a month or less? Why is it we have people living on the edge of economic insecurity? There are a number of European countries with larger populations and fewer resources which have been able to do better for their elderly people than we have been able to do for ours. How do you explain that? Surely the only explanation is that the wealth of this country is not reaching the elderly people who created it and who need it today. That, unfortunately, is the sad case.
What we are finding now, and found under the former government, is that whenever there is a deficit in government financing the only way the government can think of to solve the problem is to cut back on benefits to the elderly. 1 am afraid of the type of cutbacks that may be looming in the future. that Bill C-ll, respecting certain postal rates, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as members of this House are well aware, beginning in 1976 and continuing until 1979 the former Liberal government chose to institute increases in letter and second-class postage rates by way of authorization by the governor in council pursuant to subsection 13(b) of the Financial Administration Act, rather than by presenting a bill to Parliament amending sections 10 and 11 of the Post Office Act.
Shame!

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Postmaster General
speechtext:
On these occasions this government, when we were sitting in opposition, spoke out against the Liberal government of the day for increasing postal rates by regulation instead of amending the Post Office Act, and for ignoring critical reports of this practice by the Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
In its third report dated October 4, 1976, the Standing Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments considered that regulations setting new rates were ultra vires of section 6 of the Post Office Act and section 13 of the Financial Adminis-

tration Act. It added that the use of regulations "amount to an unusual and unexpected use of power conferred upon the governor in council by section 13 of the Financial Administration Act". The fourth and sixth reports of the same committee reiterated those objections.
On the question of legality, previous postmasters general have stated in the House and in letters to the committee that before the regulations were made legal opinion from the Department of Justice had been considered. On the one occasion when the legitimacy of using the Financial Administration Act was challenged in the courts, the decision which was rendered on August 2, 1978, was in favour of the position the former government had taken.
However, I wish to remind all hon. members that that decision is now before the Federal Court of Appeal, and I think 1 should tell the House that the decision would have been argued in that court earlier this summer had I not intervened and asked the legal officers of the government to seek an adjournment. That adjournment was granted by the plaintiffs, the appellants in this case, on my undertaking to introduce into this House legislation that would in a retroactive way legitimize the rate increases that had been made under the Financial Administration Act.
I want to say to the House that the action which was taken in the courts was a direct result of certain plaintiffs feeling that what was being done was not according to the constitution and was contrary to the proper practices of Parliament.
It ought to be obvious to all members that, despite the fact that the government had won the case in the lower court, the case was being pursued actively in the Federal Court of Appeal and would, no doubt, have gone to the Supreme Court of Canada. I think all hon. members on either side of the House will agree that for the Post office and, indeed, this government, to be left in that sort of uncertainty was just unacceptable, and as a consequence, as I have said, the adjournment was obtained on the undertaking that this legislation would be introduced. I understand that the arrangement is that if this bill should meet with the approval of the House the case will be discontinued.
But irrespective of the outcome of the current case, this government considers that there is still a need to eliminate controversy over the use of section 13(b) of the Financial Administration Act. We concur with committee criticism about unusual and unexpected use of power by previous governments, and agree that as long as amendment to the Post Office Act exists as a means of rate adjustment, the Financial Administration Act is not the preferred method of increasing letter and second class postal rates. Although the use of the regulation may be technically within the law, it is clearly less than acceptable to some members of this House, the Senate, and the Canadian public.
I need not remind this House that there are still many problems to overcome before the Post Office can be restored to its former level of pride, dignity, and service. Not the least of
October 22, 1979

these will be the conversion of the department into a Crown corporation. As I said, I hope to be introducing legislation to that effect some time after Christmas. Those problems will be much easier to tackle if this government is not at the same time fighting a rearguard battle against problems stemming from actions by the previous government.
Passage of this bill will legally confirm the amendments to the postal rates that were made by regulation by deeming them to have been made under the Post Office Act. In turn, this will clear the books and allow us to turn our full attention to the more important task of providing all Canadians with the postal service they expect and deserve.
Mr. Speaker, before I answer some of the remarks of the Postmaster General (Mr. Fraser) I congratulate him on tabling the annual report of the Post Office on time.

It was compiled under the administration of the former government. 1 read it very carefully, and I must say that it was one of the best reports I have read yet. We reduced the deficit, we increased the volume, and did many other things we could really be proud of because it was really administered as closely as possible to private administration. I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that a bill like this one, Bill C-II, as introduced by the Postmaster General at this point, intrigues me somewhat and strikes me as a strange priority. That is why I shall make a few comments and put a few brief questions, since another hon. member would like to speak to the matter; and as we want to complete the study of this bill tonight, I have promised to co-operate in that way.
I want to deal with the need for this bill.

When they were in opposition the Conservatives opposed the adjustment of postal rates under the authority of the Financial Administration Act, section 13(b), which allows the governor in council to increase rates. But with this bill the government prefers to amend sections 10 and 11 of the Post Office Act by Parliament. Despite legal opinions from the Crown that the use of the Financial Administration Act was legal, the Tories attacked our government at the time, saying that we were bypassing Parliament.
I would like to make myself clear on these points. The Department of Justice has affirmed the legality of the use of section 13 in adjusting postal rates. Moreover, when this method was tested in the courts, it was clearly upheld until there was an appeal. Something which perhaps the minister may not know is that the wording is in our Bill C-27, to convert the Post Office into a Crown corporation. The government has not invented anything.
The wording of the present bill is in our Bill C-27 and was put there in order to give the Crown corporation the certainty that there would not be obstructive or negative action from
Postal Rates
interested groups. In other words, we wanted to ensure that there would be a smooth start for the Crown corporation. It was also well known that part of the reason for the use of section 13 was to avoid taking up valuable time in a busy parliamentary schedule, and to give six months notice to postal users. However, rate increases were announced in the House of Commons and discussed there as well.
It was mentioned that we were bypassing Parliament. I found this curious coming from a government which has waited for so long before calling Parliament, the longest period in history without a Parliament. This in itself implies a criticism of the present administration's attitude to Parliament in relation to postal rates.
It is even more intriguing that the government has stated its intention to reintroduce legislation to convert Canada Post to a Crown corporation only after the Christmas recess, but yet has taken this occasion to place before us, piecemeal, a procedure for rate increases alone, which was already in our Bill C-27. Does this mean that the government is intending to introduce other postal rate increases? Does it mean that the government plans to delay or shelve introducing Crown corporation legislation, when it has had so much time to prepare or modify that legislation? Or does it mean that the government intends to modify the postal rate process further in future legislation which is well defined in C-27?
Are we going to see a series of minor bills dealing with postal operations, instead of one concise, comprehensive piece of legislation like our proposed Bill C-27? In Bill C-27, which was laid before the last Parliament by the Liberal administration, there was outlined an excellent postal rate procedure. It proposed rate changes subject to governor in council approval which then would be made public. If there were any objections, they would be filed and investigated by the Canadian Transport Commission, which would have been given the power to disallow the rate change.
Why has the government not done its home work and presented some substantial legislation to the House, addressing the real problems facing the Post Office, instead of playing a game of preferred or selective procedures? The government may well prefer to avoid using the Financial Administration Act to change postal rates, but regardless of this bill it could still change the rates if that is its intention. That is why I cannot understand the government presenting this bill now. Why did it not introduce a bill like ours to make the Post Office a Crown Corporation?
Bill C-27 is there, and with a few little changes which have been suggested by the management, it could be presented and have the same effect. It would also be a great help to the unions, the syndicates and the labour movement in the Post Office because it would prove that this government intends to move fast in implementing the legislation making the Post Office a Crown corporation, thereby getting the matter out of the way in this session.

Mr. Speaker, this is an Alice in Wonderland situation. The hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Lamontagne) lacks any credibility in any of the suggestions he makes to the government on how the Post Office should be run. For 16 years that party had a revolving-door policy with respect to most matters in the Post Office. They screwed the situation up so badly that human and interpersonnel relationships within the Post Office denied any successful means of collective bargaining.
Now the hon. member stands in this House like a Judas Iscariot and suggests to the new Postmaster General (Mr. Fraser) what he should do. Why did the hon. member not follow through with his suggestions when he had the opportunity? Why did his government bring in a Crown corporation bill in the twilight of the last Parliament if they were really serious about making the Post Office a Crown corporation, something which had been recommended by every royal commission since 1960? They brought it in during the twilight months. I think they are a phony gang, these Liberals, to suggest to the government the kinds of things that should be done.

This is implicit in this bill, and I will deal with it a little later. 1 am glad they are applauding, Mr. Speaker. They will get their chance to speak in a minute.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, the need for increased rates in the past was because there were increased costs in the Post Office, largely due to the implementation of technological change in 1971. There was $1 billion worth of technological change which was part of the recommendations of the "Blueprint for Change" in the Post Office. The Liberal government, whose representative just now made suggestions to the minister, should know that the "blueprint for change" not only envisaged changes with respect to the physical operation of the Post Office but also changes in human approaches to human problems. While they moved rapidly toward technological change in the Post Office, the whole question of the way management dealt with workers and the workers' response to technological change was neglected.
We should keep in mind that the workers in the Post Office came under the Public Service Staff Relations Act and were therefore excluded from any sort of participation in the discussion of technological change in the work place. Had they come under the Canada Labour Code they could have discussed matters and have negotiated technological change. Interhuman relationships became very abrasive and led to a breakdown in service to the Canadian people. That breakdown in

service cost a great deal of money and has required continuous increases in rates.
This government, when in opposition, had a good analysis of the problem-a super analysis of the problem. The hon. member who spoke for the Conservative party when it was in opposition travelled the world looking at post offices. Indeed, he was postmaster general in a previous Conservative government. They well knew the problems, therefore, but now that they are in office the Postmaster General is Mr. Clean. The first thing the government did was wedge the Post Office in between oil spills and acid rain.
The most serious problem in the public service today is the Post Office. Everybody recognizes that. The Post Office and those who work in it have been made a scapegoat. They have been used to whip up a kind of fascistic response to the fact that the people do not get their mail on time. We could have hoped, therefore, for a minister whose sole and full time job was to look after the Post Office and make sure there was harmony in it. He could have started from scratch. There was a clean slate. The government did not have to make apologies for the mess perpetrated on the people of Canada by the previous Liberal administration.
We like the Postmaster General. He is a nice man-he is very expansive, very absorbent, very helpful, very courteous but, Mr. Speaker, he cannot deal with Inco and acid rain and oil spills and the Post Office problem all at the same time. The minister has said there will be a Crown corporation before Christmas-but he did not say which Christmas.

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Postmaster General
speechtext: After Christmas.

Christmas 1980? Christmas 1981? We looked for a new start, a risorgimento as the Italians say-a new beginning. We did not get it. We got the minister with other responsibilities, and the Post Office is just a side issue.
When in opposition the government recognized that the interpersonal problems within the Post Office resulted in over
60,000	grievances accumulating. The Post Office management, playing games, allowed these grievances to be appealed all the way through three stages. The workers would win, the matter would go to adjudication, and on the eve of adjudication the Post Office would withdraw the grievance or not continue with it. Those accumulated grievances exacerbated relationships within the Post Office between management and the people on the floor of the plant. One would have thought that a new government that wanted to show good faith, that had no record and that did not have to apologize for the mistakes of the past, would have wiped out those 60,000 grievances. They did not. The government may be Mr. Clean in the public image but they allow the situation to continue. Those grievances still exist. Negotiations for a new contract will take place soon and those grievances can only cause problems.
One of the other problems in the Post Office-and I shall be blunt, Mr. Speaker-was the presence of a Mr. Corkery and Mr. Pare. Both gentlemen came from the private sector, one from Loebs and the other from a corporation in Hamilton.
October 22, 1979

They may know how to run a private enterprise corporation where profit is the motive, but they have a very narrow view when running something that is service oriented, where it is important for workers to get along with management. The thrust of the Post Office is to provide service to the people who pay for it, namely, taxpayers. This government did not remove those two gentlemen although they had a wonderful opportunity to do so. They could have called them Liberals; they could have shaken them out and brought in some new faces. It has been done in other departments. Maybe they were Tories in hiding, or closet Tories! Those gentlemen are still there, still mal-administering, still exacerbating the problems in the Post Office. This government acts as though nothing has changed and I suppose, politically, nothing has.
The principle established in Bill C-l 1 is one that we on this side of the House support and applaud. I recently read something interesting in a report of an interview between the head of the workers at de Havilland and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens). Crown corporations come under the Financial Administration Act, so in effect the administration of de Havilland comes under that act. The President of the Treasury Board, however, was reported as saying that any changes with respect to privatizing de Havilland would not be brought to the House of Commons. That is what he said. This is a downgrading of Parliament, an insult to Parliament, and it flies in the face of this particular principle put forward on the altar of democracy by the Postmaster General cum environment minister.

subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- MORTGAGE INSURANCE UNDERWRITING PRACTICES
CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- MORTGAGE INSURANCE UNDERWRITING PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 18 I asked the minister in charge of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation if he would assure this House that he would advise his officials in the corporation that, in view of the enormous numbers of repossession of townhouse condominiums, the corporation would cease giving undertakings to insure to lenders so that there would be no further building of this type of accommodation, certainly until the enormous surplus of repossessions were disposed of.
In answer to that question the minister gave me and this House a very unsatisfactory reply. The minister said:
Mr. Speaker, mortgage insurance underwriting practices obligate the corporation to evaluate individual applications very carefully. However, we will be extremely cautious in getting into this sort of practice until we have studied market conditions.
In March, 1978, James Crozier, for the region of Peel, filed with the regional council there and with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation a complete analysis of the social disaster that was taking place in the county and region of Peel, and indeed metropolitan Toronto, as a result of the inept housing practice of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That document, filed with the corporation, outlines the problems, the repossessions, the inability of people to make and carry through with AHOP financing, the impossibility of marketing, by way of resale, condominium townhouses. The study was over a year and a half period.
At that time, and I point out that it was well over a year and a half ago, we had already many, many condominium repossessions in the hands of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The real estate fraternity, private real estate agents, were refusing to take listings for resale of condominium townhouses. People were taking keys in and handing them to the mortgage company saying, "We cannot pay our payments," and the corporation was accepting quit claim deeds. Yet the corporation continued to give undertakings to insure and enable the start up of more and more condominium townhouse projects, to the effect the minister advises me that on July 2 of this year they had in possession, in repossessions- empty repossessions of condominium townhouses-in Mississauga alone 791 units. Just walking the streets and talking to people one can see what is happening in my city-more and more of these condominium townhouses are now in possession of the corporation.
I could give the minister projects, and he has heard about them from me before-there is one called Talka Village on the Lakeshore Road in Mississauga. That project is advertised on CTV and touted by one Joel Aldred. It is a fine development, they say. It is a designed slum with not one sale-not one legitimate sale. There is a condominium project called Balsam Woods, again on the Lakeshore Road, in my riding. It has been financed and in and out of repossession problems for the last four years. Half of the units are still unoccupied although they have been built for four years. And yet this corporation and its inept officers continue to use the provisions of the

October 22, 1979
Adjournment Debate
National Housing Act to erect more and more condominium townhouses, to destroy and completely ruin the market for that type of accommodation so that those who were unfortunate enough to have put their hard earned cash into an equity position in that type of housing, find that their equities have totally disappeared.
Indeed, to say that the corporation has an obligation to evaluate individual market conditions is an indication that the officers of the corporation are of such inept quality that their ability to evaluate has been long since lost. And so, when I asked the minister this question, a rather pressing question, particularly in view of the financial stability of Canada Housing and Mortgage Corporation, I would have expected the minister to say, "We have ceased giving undertakings to insure on condominium townhouses, certainly in the city of Mississauga."

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- MORTGAGE INSURANCE UNDERWRITING PRACTICES
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell my hon. friend that I very much appreciate the knowledge and experience he brings to this chamber in matters of housing. He has practised law. He has dealt with the situation. But I want to remind him that things are not quite as simple or direct as he would believe.
As demand for AHOP and assisted rental programs began to soften, CMHC did introduce a series of measures designed to restrict project approvals unless the need for housing was clearly identified. The corporation did initiate detailed reviews of local market situations, a check of current and pending vacancy rates, profiles of existing AHOP and ARP projects, specific need and demand surveys were instituted, and reviews of entrepreneurs' financial and development capabilities were carried out.
I would remind the hon. member that the identification of turning points in real estate markets is not always easy, particularly in advance, often when a local market forms a part of a major metropolitan market. New policy in assessing more carefully the situation pertaining to condominium town-houses has been instituted.
The hon. member has brought to my attention, as well, the practice of accepting quit claim deeds, which has not always been satisfactory. The situation there has changed as well. If an owner attempts to quit claim his property and subsequently goes into arrears, CMHC will now institute foreclosure proceedings and the owner will have to pay the legal costs and mortgage his condominium for the arrears unless there is a very good reason why he should not, for example, if the property is abandoned and there are serious mortgage arrears and no reasonable hope of recovering them, or an owner has been transferred and is beyond reasonable commuting distance. Then we would look at the quit claim deed situation and review it on its merits.
It is, I think, wrong to condemn in a blanket fashion the results of some of these programs which the previous adminis-

tration instituted. I would prefer to think they were instituted with good intentions. There is a proverb which says that the path to hell is paved with good intentions, and sometimes the results have not been what I think all of us in this chamber would have hoped. But I believe it would be a little harsh to condemn out of hand the good will and the capability of the CMHC officials. This is not to say mistakes have not been made; it is not to say we are not very interested in looking into the situation.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I appreciate the forthright and thorough way in which the hon. member has brought these matters before the House, and to assure him that I am getting the utmost co-operation from the officials of the corporation in order to alleviate these conditions, including an early marketing of considerable numbers of units, to put it mildly, in possession of which the corporation now finds itself.

subtopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING NEWSPRINT-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S INTERVENTION
COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING NEWSPRINT-REQUEST FOR MINISTER'S INTERVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 17 last, I put two questions to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), the first dealing with the scarcity of newsprint which compelled several Quebec newspapers to restrict their circulation or the number of pages in their publications and I asked the minister to study the matter thoroughly and, if he deemed it necessary, to submit the case to the director of investigation and research in the competition branch of his department to launch the required investigation.
I am pleased to say to the House tonight that I received this morning a letter from the minister advising me that he had discussed the matter with the director of investigation and research who had assured him that he would study the matter closely to see if it would be advisable to institute proceedings under the Combines Investigation Act. I am satisfied with the step taken by the minister and I thank him.
I must say that the scarcity of newsprint for newspapers in Quebec appears as ridiculous as oil shortages in Alberta. Quebec is enormously well endowed with forest resources and it is unimaginable that Quebec industries cannot get all the necessary paper. There is perhaps an explanation to this situation that may be due to market conditions more than to some anti-competitive behaviour. I noted quite recently an article which appeared in Le Devoir to the effect that the pulp and paper industry in Canada has known a tremendous development these past few months, and I quote:
The major part of our pulp and paper production is being exported to the United States where the demand for newsprint and pulp and paper by products has considerably increased, thereby giving a new impetus to our industry. These exports, paid in U.S. dollars of much greater value than Canadian dollars, are responsible for an exceptional increase in the profits of the pulp and paper industry.
October 22, 1979

I am delighted for the pulp and paper industry. 1 have of course no objection to these companies making profits, but I am concerned that they fail perhaps to provide an essential service and to meet the Canadian demand. And I suggest that it is imperative, in the context of fair competition in Canada, that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs tackle this problem and try to find a short-term solution in particular to the pulp and paper shortage in Quebec.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind this House that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs himself admitted that there would be serious loopholes in the Combines Investigation Act. And I asked the minister in this House whether he intended to bring in amendments to that legislation. He answered that his government was urgently considering several matters that were not referred to in the Speech from the Throne. That answer appears somewhat vague to me. On the one hand, he finds the legislation porous and he even goes so far as to say that certain large corporations could abuse the act and go unpunished. On the other hand, he does not see fit to announce the intention of his government to amend the Combines Investigation Act. 1 think it is important for the minister to give us actual signs of his intentions in this respect. Is he going to protect the interest of Canadian consumers or is he going to abdicate his responsibilities in face of the Progressive Conservative lobbying in this country which, as you know, Mr. Speaker, has always opposed amending the Canadian Competition Act. I hope the minister will take positive action and will not limit himself to pious statements and will introduce in the House a competition act with teeth. 1 can assure him of my support and the support of the members on this side of the House if, as a Progressive Conservative minister, he has the courage to face the music and even stand against some of his colleagues on the government side and decides to introduce a good competition measure in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to thank the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) for his question and for giving me the opportunity to respond for the first time in the House. In particular, 1 should like to thank him for the subject he has chosen and for the very important nature of the question in terms of the ability of the newspaper industry in Quebec to respond to the needs of the Quebec people.
1 would like to refer the hon. member in particular to the letter sent to him on October 19 by the minister, in which the following is stated:
Adjournment Debate
On two previous occasions this year, problems similar to that of Le Journal's were brought to the director's attention. In one instance, the director found that newsprint was generally in short supply, but that the shortage was due to market conditions and not anti-competitive behaviour. It is probable that this situation persists to the present. The second instance involved weekly local and regional newspapers in Quebec who were experiencing difficulty in obtaining adequate newsprint supplies. The director discussed the matter with the Quebec government officials who had alerted him to the problem. Meetings were also held between those officials and representatives of the industry and newspapers. As a result, the temporary shortage was resolved satisfactorily.
Now I should like to refer quickly to an article in today's Gazette in which the following is stated:
Quebecor-
The publisher of Montreal's biggest daily newspaper
-has been hit harder than any other large Canadian newspaper publisher by the newsprint shortage, which has been building for the past year as growing publishers' consumption of newsprint wiped out excess productive capacity in the newsprint industry.
The Journal de Montreal now sells about 325,000 copies a day, up from 200,000 copies last year. I think this clearly shows that it is a supply problem. In fact, contracts have been honoured, new supplies have been found, for a paper whose 1977 consumption was 65,000 tons and whose 1979 consumption will be 79,000 tons of newsprint. Provisions have been made for an extra 3,000 tons monthly of newsprint through one of the Journal de Montreal's existing suppliers. Expansion and building will create new supply early next year.
As the former minister will know, there are no provisions in the Combines Investigation Act to deal with this matter of proof in terms of shortage of supplies. The act is essentially as it was under the former administration. If the hon. member for Papineau has specific references which he feels are the proper domain of the director of investigation and research, I have been assured that the director will accept and assess them. In the meantime the director will continue to monitor the situation to discern any evidence of price fixing, collusion, or any other behaviour which might be detrimental to our free market system. On a specific matter of revision or amendments to the act, I must defer to the minister and will be happy to respond in writing to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) a very simple question about Canada's position relative to continuing its program of challenge and leadership to encourage Canadians to sponsor families of refugees from Vietnam. His answer was so evasive and unsatisfactory that I want to take the opportunity this evening to take my question very clear, although 1 think it was very clear this afternoon, and to give the minister or his parliamentary secretary an opportunity to tell Canadians precisely what their government intends to do now that the 50,000 quota offered by the government has been met by almost a full response from the Canadian people, and where we go from here.
The minister takes enormous pride in the sponsorship program created by him and his colleague, the Secretary of State

October 22, 1979
Adjournment Debate
for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald), this summer. I think it is a good program. 1 am not critical of it, but 1 do not take nearly the satisfaction from it that he does.
Repeatedly he has said that it is the most generous program in the world for dealing with Vietnamese refugees. Those are not the facts, as I understand them. I should like to take a moment of my time to set out the facts which I had from a very authoritative source at a conference on the boat people last Friday. As of mid-October, the United States had admitted and Landed 260,000 boat people; China had admitted
250.000	people; France had admitted 59,000 boat people; Australia had admitted 25,551 southeast Asians of whom
19.000	were boat people; and Canada had admitted 22,348. That is a good total, but it is certainly not the world's record. It is not the world's record in absolute terms, per capita terms, nor in terms of accommodation per square mile of the host country. It is very far from it. I am not suggesting these criteria, but I want to remind the minister that this is far from being the most generous refugee reception program in the world.
This afternoon I asked him where the government was going from here, and this is what I meant by that. As he indicated, we have close to 20,000 private sponsorships. Now, 4,000 should be allocated from an earlier period. This is the way the commission is calculating this figure. In effect we are very close to having 25,000 private sponsorships. We may well have it within a week. That means the 25,000 public sponsorships to be matched on a one to one basis, which the government put forward as its challenge to the Canadian people, are virtually all committed. So the question arises: where do we go from here? I know they are not all here in Canada. I have figures which indicate that only 22,348 are here in Canada at this time.
Is the minister saying that no more private sponsorships will be encouraged from now on, and that until all of these already committed people arrive we cannot look to the government for any further leadership or challenge to the Canadian people? Is that what the minister is saying? If it is, I think he should just say it and accept the responsibility for it, instead of going off and talking about how complicated his program is and how busy he is handling the flow of Vietnamese refugees who are already committed.
I want the minister or his parliamentary secretary, who I am glad to see in the Flouse, to tell us where the government is going from here in providing leadership and challenge to the
Canadian people. If nothing more is being done, if there is not going to be anything more to encourage private sponsorships, will the minister assure the House that, having backed down on providing leadership and challenge, he will at least not prevent people in the private sector from continuing to sponsor new families of boat people or Vietnamese refugees?
The flow out of Vietnam is very low right now. The monsoons are on and we do not know whether, when the monsoons end, the levels of immigration will go up to the levels at the end of the Geneva Conference. We do not know if they will even go up to the levels they were at before that. The level may be high, but this government ought to have a policy. Instead of waffling and telling us how busy he is, the minister should tell us what the Canadian government plans to do next.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to remind the hon. member opposite that in speaking for the minister on Friday I did not say, as he indicated in his question, that nothing more could be done until the 50,000 Indochinese refugees had arrived in Canada. I did indicate that we were now well on the way to receiving sufficient sponsorship undertakings from Canadian voluntary groups to ensure that our 50,000 refugee target will be met by the end of 1980 in accordance with the government-voluntary partnership formula announced in July, and that our prime thrust was to ensure that our goal was met and the program was seen to be a success.
Members will recall that the 50,000 target was composed of the 8,000 originally pledged by the government for 1979, plus
21.000	voluntary sponsorships matched by 21,000 government refugees.
It should be pointed out, however, that to date less than
15.000	Indochinese refugees have been brought to Canada, and a major challenge, therefore, remains in bringing the remaining 35,000 Indochinese to Canada and successfully establishing them here through the joint efforts of the government and voluntary groups. There is a question as to the implications of possible voluntary sponsorships beyond the
21.000	needed to reach the 50,000 total.
That is the question I asked.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: This question is now under active study by the government and an announcement will be made at an early date once the voluntary undertaking target has been met.
